### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

This paper is the first individual-level administrative-data account of the 2024–25 Better FAFSA rollout in a large state, and its durable contribution is a decomposition that the aggregate national trackers could not make: California FAFSA submissions rose by under 1% overall (537,112 vs. 533,221 in a 25% sample) while freshman submissions fell about 7% — about 13% by the state aid deadline — and continuing-student submissions rose 6–14%; and among students who had entered the system under the old form, refiling fell modestly but consistently across every education level, dependency status, and public sector. Readers can rely on those descriptive facts, which reproduce from the paper's own Table 1 and hold up across Tables 2–4, and should cite the paper for them. They should not lean on the paper's causal magnitudes, its equity gradient, or its two most quotable inferences. The refiling design has no untreated comparison group and its own stated validation check fails — the pre-period cohort coefficient the authors expected to be near zero is significantly positive in nearly every cell and often larger than the treatment coefficient — so the refiling effect is a range (roughly 2–4 pp) rather than the 1.7 pp the text emphasizes, and every ranking of who was hurt most flips when the pre-trend is subtracted. The claim that the policy hurt families "facing the steepest barriers" rests on a single zip-code racial-composition proxy reported only in the online appendix, with no matching gradient across income terciles. The reassuring result that state aid receipt and reenrollment rose is estimated only among prior-year recipients and enrollees, only in the three public systems, and shows cohort-to-cohort swings (CSU reenrollment −3.1 to +4.8 pp) that no FAFSA mechanism explains. And the abstract's suggestion that students are "enrolling, but without the support of state or federal financial aid" is not observed anywhere — the data contain no federal aid outcome and no enrollment measure for the freshmen whose filings fell. Two text–table disagreements that survived production (the Table 3 Cal Grant paragraph and the freshman refile baseline), an inconsistent cohort-labeling scheme, and the absence of a data availability statement, code, or regression sample sizes mean readers should quote numbers from the tables, never from the prose. Read it as a candid, well-scoped descriptive baseline that establishes what happened in California and frames the questions — not as a paper that settles effects.

> **Correction (2026-09-26).** The range is wider than stated, and the Methods sub-review's "linear-trend counterfactual" label for the 3.9 pp figure is wrong. β2 − β1 assumes the 2024 cohort would have matched the 2023 cohort's level; a linear extrapolation of the pre-period rise is β2 − 2β1, which is −6.1 pp for all filers. The refiling decline is therefore −1.7 pp under a flat counterfactual, −3.9 pp at the 2023 level, −6.1 pp under a linear trend, and under 1.7 pp if the pre-period rise was about to revert. The point that the sign is solid and the magnitude depends on the counterfactual stands. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against Table 2.

#### Key Strengths

- **Genuinely new microdata on a question otherwise covered only by aggregate counts.** A 25% person-level sample of CSAC FAFSA records (~500K per year, 2021–22 through 2024–25) with submission dates, Cal Grant receipt, and public-sector enrollment linked at the individual level permits the freshman/continuing decomposition and the longitudinal refiling analysis that NCAN, FSA, and NSC trackers structurally cannot support. The freshman-versus-continuing split materially corrects the reassuring "volume held up" headline.
- **The refiling-cohort design is a sensible construction for the continuing-student margin.** All three cohorts first filed under the old FAFSA, so baseline covariates — including income, which becomes unobservable in 2024 — are measured under a consistent regime, and compositional change in who first enters is held fixed. The continuing-student margin is one the public discourse largely ignored, and this is likely the best available evidence on it.
- **Linkage to downstream outcomes.** Following refilers into state aid payment and public reenrollment is what turns a filing-count paper into one that can speak, at least partially, to whether the disruption mattered.
- **Unusual candor about what the design can and cannot do.** The authors label the study descriptive, round percent changes to whole numbers to avoid false precision, acknowledge the positive pre-trend and its implication in both directions, warn about ecological bias in zip proxies, note that new students' outcomes are unobserved, point to the 2025–26 rebound in footnote 8 even though it deflates the alarm, and explicitly leave the counterfactual to the reader.
- **The descriptive half is auditable from the printed article.** The +0.73% overall change, the −7.0% freshman decline, and footnote 5's population counts all reproduce from Table 1's Ns and shares, and Table 4's text claims reproduce line by line.

#### Key Concerns

- **Identification: no comparison group and a failed pre-period check.** Better FAFSA was national, so the cohort regression is a controlled before/after, not a difference-in-differences. The paper states β1 should be near zero; it is +.022 overall (vs. −.017 for treatment), +.028 for freshmen, +.034 for independents, +.037 in the low-propensity tercile — all p<.01. The magnitude of the refiling effect therefore spans roughly −0.6 to −4.3 pp depending on the assumed counterfactual, and the distributional conclusions (Table 3 terciles, dependents vs. independents, sectors) reverse when β2−β1 is used instead of β2. The paper applies trend-adjustment in only one paragraph. Significance stars reflect sampling precision with N≈500K, not confidence about the counterfactual.
- **The equity claim rests on one ecological proxy that the paper's other proxies do not corroborate.** Freshman declines were a uniform 6–8% across all three zip income terciles; the gradient (+2% vs. −8%) appears only in the zip non-white-share cut, which pools Asian, Black, and Hispanic populations, is flagged by the authors for ecological bias, and lives entirely in appendix Tables A2 and A7. A separate Hispanic-share cut reports +11% for freshmen in the lowest tercile, which does not reconcile with the +2% figure in the main text. The mixed-status mechanism invoked (~10% of applicants) is never observed.
- **The reassuring enrollment and aid-receipt results are the least identified part of the paper, and the abstract overstates them.** Table 4 Panels B–C condition on prior-year aid receipt / public enrollment (conditioning sets that themselves changed across cohorts), cover only CC/CSU/UC (private and out-of-state enrollment unobserved, so sectoral substitution away from FAFSA-dependent privates would register as a gain), and coincide with two co-interventions — the Cal Grant deadline extension to June 2 and CSAC's active mitigation — designed to protect exactly these outcomes. The Discussion's inference that non-refilers "were unlikely to have continued their enrollment regardless" compares differently conditioned panels and cannot be identified from cohort means. The abstract's "enrolling, but without the support of state or federal financial aid" has no observed federal aid outcome and no enrollment outcome for freshmen behind it.
- **Text–table disagreements and labeling churn.** The Table 3 Cal Grant paragraph reports declines of 2.9/1.1/2.0 pp (8%/4%/4%) for middle/low/high terciles; the table shows −.020, −.001 (not significant), −.027, and no differencing recovers the text's numbers. The freshman refile sentence uses the All-column baseline (57.7% → 56.0%) where the freshman baseline is 53.1% (→ 51.4%). Cohorts are labeled by refiling year in tables, first-filing year in the equation, and calendar years matching neither in the dependency paragraph. The prior-prior year reform is misdescribed (it uses income from two years prior, not one), and the NSC citation is dated 2024, titled Spring 2025, and used for fall 2024 — a statistic NSC publicly corrected in early 2025.
- **Reproducibility falls short of 2026 journal norms.** No data availability statement or access pathway, no code or replication package, no named software, no IRB statement, no sample sizes or cluster counts in Tables 2–4, an "e.g."-only control list that differs between text and table notes, an unnamed estimator, an ambiguously worded 25% sampling rule (footnote 3), an unstated ACS vintage and tercile-construction rule, and a left-censored 2021 "first-filer" cohort that cannot be verified as first-time. Roughly a third of the quantitative claims — including the equity result and the robustness checks in footnote 6 — exist only in an online appendix.

#### What to Rely On

- **The overall-vs-freshman decomposition of 2024–25 California FAFSA submissions.** Total submissions rose just under 1% while freshman submissions fell ~7% and sophomore/upper-division submissions rose ~14%/~6%. This reproduces from Table 1 (537,112 vs. 533,221; 277K → 258K freshmen) and is the paper's most durable fact. Anchor it to its 2023 base year, which was a post-COVID peak; 2024 freshman submissions still exceeded 2021 and 2022.
- **Freshman submissions by the state aid deadline fell ~13%, versus gains of ~13% for sophomores and ~5% for upper-division students.** This is the finding with the clearest stakes (Cal Grant eligibility worth ~\$6,500–\$17,000 a year), and it is conservative in calendar time because the 2024 deadline was extended from March 2 to June 2.
- **Refiling among continuing students fell in the Better FAFSA year on both the any-refile and on-time margins, in every education level, dependency status, and public sector.** The direction is robust across Tables 2–4 Panel A; cite the magnitude as roughly 2–4 percentage points (3–4% or more relative), not as 1.7 pp.
- **Among students who received a Cal Grant or were enrolled in a California public college the prior year, aid receipt and reenrollment did not fall in 2024–25** (Table 4 Panels B–C). Cite this as a conditional descriptive fact about outcomes, not as evidence that the disruption was harmless or that non-refilers were marginal students.
- **The composition of California FAFSA filers shifted toward incumbents in 2024–25** — roughly 73,000 fewer first-time applicants offset by roughly 87,000 additional continuing filers (footnote 5, scaled from the 25% sample).
- **The implementation narrative** (three-month launch delay, mixed-status families blocked from electronic submission, 4 million unanswered calls, corrections unavailable until late June, the June 2 Cal Grant extension) is sourced to the GAO report and CSAC and is a reliable case description of a well-theorized simplification undermined by execution.
- **The paper's own statements of limitation** — no individual income after 2024, no individual race/ethnicity, no private or out-of-state enrollment, no outcomes for new students, CDAA filers excluded, mixed-status families unidentifiable — are accurate and should travel with any citation.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- **"Refiling fell 1.7 percentage points."** There is no untreated comparison group and the pre-period coefficient is +2.2 pp, so the effect is a range (≈ −0.6 to −4.3 pp across cells and counterfactuals), not a point estimate.
- **Any ranking of who was hurt most in refiling** (Table 3 propensity terciles, dependents vs. independents, UC vs. CSU vs. CCC). Baseline-relative, the disruption looks concentrated among mid/high-propensity and dependent students; trend-adjusted (β2−β1), it is flat or worse for low-propensity and independent students, and roughly twice as large at CCC. Recompute before citing.
- **"The policy negatively impacted families that already faced the steepest barriers."** Supported only by a zip-level non-white-share cut in the appendix; income and SNAP terciles show no gradient; the Hispanic-share and non-white-share figures in the text do not reconcile; the mixed-status mechanism is unobserved. Cite as a neighborhood-composition pattern, not a student-level racial gradient.
- **"Many students may be enrolling, but without the support of state or federal financial aid."** No federal aid or Pell outcome exists in the data, no enrollment is observed for the freshmen whose filings fell, private/out-of-state enrollment is unobserved, and CDAA filers are excluded. This is an inference from a missing-applications count, not a finding.
- **"Enrollment and aid receipt rose despite the disruption" / "non-refilers were not coming back anyway."** Conditioned on prior-year receipt/enrollment, public-sector only, subject to a sectoral-substitution explanation, coincident with the deadline extension and CSAC mitigation, and estimated from panels whose cohort-to-cohort swings (CSU reenrollment −3.1 to +4.8 pp) dwarf any plausible FAFSA effect. The selection inference compares differently conditioned samples and is not identified.
- **The Table 3 Cal Grant paragraph (2.9 / 1.1 / 2.0 pp; 8% / 4% / 4%).** These numbers do not appear in Table 3, which shows −.020 / −.001 (ns) / −.027. The honest statement for the lowest tercile is no detectable change.
- **The freshman refile path "57.7% to 56.0%."** That is the All column; the freshman baseline is 53.1% → 51.4%. Use the Cal Grant version (32.9% base, −1.9 pp, ~6%) if one freshman number is needed — it is stated correctly.
- **Calendar years in the dependency-status paragraph** ("65.7% in 2024 to 63.3% in 2025"; "47.8% in 2025"). The arithmetic is right; the years are not. These are regression-adjusted contrasts against a baseline two cohorts back, not raw year-over-year changes.
- **The sophomore surge (+14%) as evidence that continuing students navigated Better FAFSA easily.** Partly mechanical: the unusually large 2023 freshman cohort (52% share vs. 47–48% in other years) feeds a larger 2024 sophomore pool.
- **The prior-prior year description and the NSC citation.** PPY moved to income data from two years prior, not one; the NSC reference is mislabeled and its fall 2024 freshman figure was publicly revised. Verify both at source before repeating.
- **Significance stars in Tables 2–4.** With N≈500K everything is p<.01; the stars measure within-cohort sampling precision, not uncertainty about the counterfactual, which is unquantified and far larger.
- **California as representative.** The state extended its deadline three months, offers unusually generous state aid, ran an active mitigation effort, and routes undocumented students out of the data. Its estimates are plausibly a lower bound on disruption elsewhere, not an average.
- **Anything sourced to the online appendix** (Tables A2–A7: the zip-code submission changes, the propensity model, the random-forest check, the enrollment disaggregation, the school-fixed-effects robustness in footnote 6). None of it is verifiable from the article; fetch the supplement before building on it.
- **The college-level mandatory-FAFSA recommendation.** Its citations concern high-school mandates, and it conflicts with the paper's own reading that non-refilers were not returning anyway. Auto-renewal for returning students is the recommendation the evidence actually supports.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This is an honestly-labeled descriptive study built on excellent administrative data (a 25% sample of California FAFSA applications, ~500K/year, 2021–22 through 2024–25), and its core descriptive facts about who did and did not file are trustworthy. But the central regression's identifying logic fails on the paper's own terms — the pre-period cohort coefficient the authors expected to be near zero is significantly positive in nearly every cell, and typically larger in magnitude than the treatment coefficient — so the magnitude and the distributional pattern of the refiling declines depend heavily on which counterfactual trend a reader assumes. The enrollment and aid-receipt results in Table 4 Panels B–C are the weakest part of the paper and should not be read as evidence that Better FAFSA left enrollment unharmed.

**Strengths:**

- Data are a genuine asset: near-universal state administrative records from the California Student Aid Commission covering four application cycles, with FAFSA submission dates, Cal Grant receipt, and public-sector enrollment linked at the individual level. Sample sizes (510K–537K per year) make the descriptive series precise, and the year-over-year N pattern (533,221 → 537,112) is internally consistent with the reported ~1% overall submission increase.
- The cohort design is well-chosen for the one thing it can do: all three refiling cohorts first filed under the OLD FAFSA (2021, 2022, 2023 first-filers), so baseline covariates — including family income, which becomes unobservable in 2024 — are measured under a consistent regime for every cohort. This neatly sidesteps the 2024 data loss for the regression analysis even though it cripples the descriptive analysis.
- Repeated, unusually candid self-limitation. The Methods section explicitly disclaims causal attribution for the descriptive comparisons ("we cannot differentiate between the impacts of Better FAFSA and other secular trends"), rounds percent changes to whole numbers "so as not to overstate precision," and the Discussion tells readers directly that if pre-trends were rising the effects are understated and if reverting, overstated — "We leave it to the reader to consider."
- The predicted-refiling-propensity analysis (Table 3), which fits a logistic model on 2021–22 characteristics and then scores later cohorts, is a sensible guard against the most obvious composition threat — that the 2023 first-filer cohort was swollen with marginal applicants during the post-COVID rebound (freshman share rose from 47% to 52% by 2023).
- The paper flags the family-size measurement break (3.03 → 3.53) as an artifact of Better FAFSA pulling exemptions from tax records rather than self-report, and is upfront that zip-code race and income measures are ecological proxies subject to reversal at the individual level.

**Weaknesses:**

- The stated validation test fails. The paper writes "We expect that β1 will remain close to zero... This finding provides additional evidence allowing us to attribute changes in refiling behavior directly to the Better FAFSA." In fact the 2023-cohort coefficient is significantly positive nearly everywhere and often exceeds |β2|: +.022 (SE .001) overall vs. −.017 for treatment in Table 2A; +.034 vs. −.011 for independent students; +.037 vs. −.006 in the low-propensity tercile (Table 3). The authors' own pre-period contradicts the flat-counterfactual assumption their design requires.
- Because the pre-trend is non-zero, the distributional conclusions flip depending on framing, and the prose headlines only one framing. Relative to the 2022-cohort baseline, Table 3 reads as declines concentrated among mid/high-propensity refilers (−2.4, −2.7 pp) and barely touching the low tercile (−0.6 pp). Trend-adjusted (β2−β1), the declines are −.043, −.042, −.033 — essentially flat or slightly LARGER for the low-propensity group. Same reversal in Table 2B: baseline-relative, dependent students look harder-hit (−2.4 vs −1.1 pp) and independents show "no change" on the Cal Grant deadline (−.000); trend-adjusted, independents fare worse on both (−.045 and −.023).
- Table 4 Panel C (enrollment) is not identified. The pre-period cohort movement is larger than any plausible treatment effect: CSU reenrollment swings from −.031 (2023 cohort) to +.048 (2024 cohort), an 8 pp swing across three cohorts, dwarfing every refiling estimate in the paper. Trend-adjusted, the CCC enrollment "gain" vanishes entirely (+.018 → +.019, difference +.001) while CSU's becomes an implausible +.079. Cohort-to-cohort enrollment variation is clearly driven by sector dynamics unrelated to FAFSA, so this design has essentially no power to isolate a FAFSA effect on enrollment.
- The enrollment outcome is public-sector-only. CSAC has "no data on in-state private or out-of-state enrollment." Better FAFSA's delayed ISIR delivery plausibly hurt private colleges most (they depend most on FAFSA-driven institutional aid packaging). A student shifted from a CA private to a CSU would register as an enrollment GAIN here while total enrollment was flat or falling. The paper's most quotable finding — enrollment rose despite refiling falling — has an unaddressed compositional explanation.
- The "refiled by the Cal Grant deadline" outcome uses a year-specific deadline: March 2 in pre-policy years, extended to June 2 in the treated year. The treated cohort gets a three-month-longer window, so the level is not comparable across years and the observed on-time declines (−1.4 to −2.6 pp) understate the calendar-time disruption. The paper mentions the extension in the California Context section but does not flag it when interpreting these coefficients.
- The equity finding — the paper's most policy-salient claim — rests entirely on ecological inference from zip-code racial composition, and the more reliable proxy contradicts it. Freshman submission declines were 6–8% in ALL THREE zip income terciles (no gradient), while the non-white-share cut shows +2% vs. −8%. The one measure showing a gradient is the one most exposed to ecological bias, and "non-white share" pools Asian, Black, and Hispanic populations with very different college-going patterns. The underlying estimates live in appendix Tables A2 and A7, not the main text.
- Standard errors are clustered at the zip code but the treatment varies at the cohort level — a single aggregate shock with no untreated comparison group (Better FAFSA was national). The reported SEs (.001–.005) measure within-cohort sampling precision, not uncertainty about the counterfactual, so the ubiquitous p<.01 stars badly overstate what is known.
- Tables 2–4 report no sample sizes, no control-set enumeration beyond "e.g., age, dependency status, family size" and "zip-code-level socioeconomic factors," and no fit statistics. A reader cannot tell how many students are in, say, the UC cell or the low-propensity tercile. Footnote 3 ("We select 25% of individuals from the sample so they are observed in all years") is ambiguously worded — read literally it would imply conditioning on the outcome — though the reported refiling rates of 56–60% and the year-to-year N variation rule out that reading.
- Table 4 Panels B–C condition on prior-year state aid receipt / public enrollment, and the size of that conditioning set changed across cohorts (overall enrollment rose 48% → 51%). The conditioned samples are therefore not composition-constant across cohorts.
- Mixed-status families — the group most mechanically harmed by the missing-parental-SSN problem, estimated at ~10% of applicants — are in the data but unidentifiable, and undocumented students (CDAA filers) are excluded entirely. All estimates average over a subgroup with plausibly much larger effects that cannot be separated out.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read the sign of the refiling decline as solid and the magnitude as a range, not a point. Under the paper's flat counterfactual, overall refiling fell 1.7 pp; under a linear-trend counterfactual extrapolating the +2.2 pp gain between the first two cohorts, roughly 3.9 pp; under mean reversion, less than 1.7 pp. Cite "refiling fell by roughly 2 to 4 percentage points," not "1.7 percentage points."

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The range is wider than stated, and the Methods sub-review's "linear-trend counterfactual" label for the 3.9 pp figure is wrong. β2 − β1 assumes the 2024 cohort would have matched the 2023 cohort's level; a linear extrapolation of the pre-period rise is β2 − 2β1, which is −6.1 pp for all filers. The refiling decline is therefore −1.7 pp under a flat counterfactual, −3.9 pp at the 2023 level, −6.1 pp under a linear trend, and under 1.7 pp if the pre-period rise was about to revert. The point that the sign is solid and the magnitude depends on the counterfactual stands. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against Table 2.

- Do NOT cite the Table 3 result as evidence that Better FAFSA spared the least-attached students. That conclusion holds only in the baseline-relative framing. Compute β2−β1 yourself (−.043 low, −.042 middle, −.033 high) and you get the opposite ordering. The paper reports both, but the prose emphasizes the framing that gives the more intuitive answer.
- Treat Table 4 Panel C as a description of California public-sector enrollment trends, not as a Better FAFSA effect. The −3.1 pp → +4.8 pp CSU swing across three cohorts is too large and too clearly non-FAFSA to support the inference. Specifically, do not repeat the paper's Discussion claim that null/positive aid and enrollment results "suggest that students negatively affected by the change to Better FAFSA were unlikely to have continued their enrollment regardless" — that is a claim about who the compliers were, which aggregate cohort means cannot identify.
- Before citing "enrollment rose despite the FAFSA disruption," note that enrollment here means CA public (CC/CSU/UC) only. Pair it with an independent source covering private and out-of-state enrollment; a public-sector gain is consistent with sectoral substitution away from FAFSA-dependent private colleges.
- Ignore the significance stars. With ~500K observations everything is p<.01; the stars describe sampling precision within a cohort, not confidence that a change was caused by Better FAFSA. The relevant uncertainty — what 2024 would have looked like absent the policy — is unquantified and orders of magnitude larger.
- The descriptive freshman decline (−7% overall, −13% by the state aid deadline) is the paper's most robust and most citable finding, but anchor it correctly: the base year (2023) was an unusual post-COVID peak (freshman share 52% vs. 47–48% in other years), and the paper concedes 2024 freshman submissions were "slightly higher than in 2021 and 2022." The decline is real relative to 2023; the 7% figure is base-year sensitive.
- Discount the sophomore/upper-division surge (+14%, +6%) as partly mechanical. The 2023 first-time cohort was unusually large, so a larger 2024 sophomore pool follows arithmetically. This is not evidence that continuing students navigated Better FAFSA easily.
- When citing the equity result, cite it as a neighborhood-composition pattern, not a student-level racial gradient — and note explicitly that the zip income terciles showed no differential (6–8% freshman declines across all three). If the finding is load-bearing for your argument, pull appendix Tables A2 and A7 and check whether the Hispanic-share cut survives at the individual level in any other data source.
- The Cal Grant on-time results are conservative, not inflated: the treated year's deadline was June 2 rather than March 2, so the treated cohort had three extra months to clear the same bar. A reader should treat the −1.4 to −2.6 pp on-time declines as a lower bound on filing-timing disruption.
- Verify against the appendix before building on: footnote 6's school-fixed-effects robustness check (Table A6), the random-forest alternative to the propensity terciles (Table A4), the logistic propensity model (A3), and the submission-change estimates the Results narrate but never tabulate in the main text (A2, A5, A7). A substantial share of the paper's quantitative claims — including the headline equity result — is only visible in the online supplement.
- For a subgroup most likely to be badly served by these averages, note the ~10% of applicants from mixed-status families who faced a manual, weeks-long submission process; they are pooled into every estimate and their effects are almost certainly larger than reported. Undocumented CDAA filers are outside the data entirely.

**Detailed Commentary:**

**What the design is, and what it identifies.** The paper runs two analyses. The first is a purely descriptive year-over-year comparison of cumulative FAFSA submissions (Figures 1–2, appendix Table A2). The authors are explicit that this cannot separate Better FAFSA from post-COVID secular trends, and they behave accordingly — rounding to whole percentage points, focusing on large divergences, and declining to interpret small ones. That is the right posture and readers should extend it: the descriptive results establish that freshman filing fell (~7% overall, ~13% by the state deadline) while continuing-student filing rose (14% sophomore, 6% upper-division), and that the composition of who files shifted toward returning students. Those facts are solid. Attribution to Better FAFSA is a judgment call the paper openly leaves to the reader.

One mechanical caveat the paper does not raise: the sophomore surge is partly arithmetic. Table 1 shows the freshman share rose from 47% (2021) to 52% (2023) before falling to 48% (2024). A larger 2023 entering cohort mechanically produces a larger 2024 sophomore pool. Symmetrically, the 2024 freshman decline is measured off an unusually high 2023 base — and the paper concedes 2024 freshman submissions exceeded both 2021 and 2022. The direction of the freshman finding is robust; the −7% magnitude is base-year sensitive.

**The cohort regression and its failed validation.** The refiling analysis (Equation 1, p. 5) regresses refiling outcomes on dummies for first-filing in 2022 and 2023 relative to 2021 first-filers, with controls and zip-clustered SEs. Only the last group refiles under Better FAFSA. This is a pre-post comparison across three first-filing cohorts, not a difference-in-differences: because Better FAFSA was national, there is no untreated comparison group anywhere. The paper does not pretend otherwise.

The design's stated internal check is that β1 (the 2022 first-filer / "2023 Cohort" row) should be near zero. The paper writes: "We expect that β1 will remain close to zero... This finding provides additional evidence allowing us to attribute changes in refiling behavior directly to the Better FAFSA policy." That check fails. In Table 2 Panel A, β1 = +.022 (SE .001) overall, +.028 for freshmen, +.016 for sophomores and upper-division — all p<.01, and all larger in absolute value than the corresponding treatment coefficients (−.017, −.017, −.018, −.019). Panel B: β1 = +.011 for dependents and +.034 for independents. Table 3: +.037, +.018, +.006 across propensity terciles. Table 4 Panel A: +.019 for CCC. The cohort trend the design assumes away is real, positive, and frequently the dominant term.

The authors notice this and reframe it — "The declines could be understated, as we observe increases in refiling rates between the 2021 and 2022 cohorts" — and in the Table 3 discussion they report the trend-adjusted figures ("all groups showed declines of roughly 3.3 to 4.3 percentage points"). That is candid. But the reframing is itself an assumption: whether the 2022→2023 cohort improvement would have continued into 2024 is exactly what cannot be known with three cohorts and no control group. The practical consequence is that the treatment magnitude is bounded roughly between −0.6 pp (Table 3 low tercile, baseline-relative) and −4.3 pp (same cell, trend-adjusted). The sign survives everywhere; the magnitude does not.

**The framing flip.** More consequential than the magnitude is that the paper's distributional conclusions are framing-dependent, and the prose consistently headlines the baseline-relative version. Table 3, baseline-relative: refiling fell 2.4 pp (middle) and 2.7 pp (high) but only 0.6 pp (low), which the text reads as the disruption sparing the least-attached. Trend-adjusted (β2 − β1): −.043 (low), −.042 (middle), −.033 (high) — flat, if anything slightly worse for the low-propensity group. The same reversal appears in Table 2 Panel B: baseline-relative, dependents look harder hit (−.024 vs −.011) and independents show literally no on-time change (−.000); trend-adjusted, independents fare worse on both margins (−.045 and −.023). And in Table 4 Panel A, sector declines look "relatively equal... at just over two percentage points" baseline-relative, but trend-adjusted are −.018 (UC), −.023 (CSU), −.041 (CCC) — community college students roughly twice as affected. To the authors' credit they flag exactly this for CCC ("Given that CCC refile rates increased from the 2022 to 2023 cohort, the decline in 2024 could be considered more substantial") and for UC's Cal Grant result ("much of this decline is already reflected in the prior year"), which trend-adjusts to +.001. But the flag is applied unevenly, and any reader citing a distributional claim from this paper should recompute β2 − β1 before doing so.

**Table 4 Panels B–C: the weakest link.** The paper's most quotable claim — that state aid receipt and enrollment rose even as refiling fell — is the least supported. In Panel C, the CSU reenrollment coefficient moves from −.031 (2023 cohort) to +.048 (2024 cohort): an 8-percentage-point swing across three adjacent cohorts, roughly four times the size of any refiling estimate in the paper. Trend-adjusted, the CCC enrollment gain evaporates (+.018 → +.019, a difference of +.001) while CSU's becomes +.079, which no FAFSA mechanism can produce. What this pattern shows is that cohort-to-cohort variation in reenrollment is dominated by sector-specific admissions and capacity dynamics of larger magnitude than any plausible FAFSA effect — which is precisely the failure condition for this identification strategy. Panel C should be read as a description of California public enrollment trends, not as an effect.

Compounding this, the enrollment outcome is public-sector-only: CSAC "has snapshot data on fall enrollment in the entire community college, CSU, and UC systems, but no data on in-state private or out-of-state enrollment." Better FAFSA's delayed ISIR delivery plausibly hit private institutions hardest, since they package the most institutional aid off FAFSA data. Substitution from CA privates into CSU would register here as an enrollment gain while total enrollment was flat. This alternative explanation is not addressed. Panel B (aid receipt: +.014, +.010, +.015) has a related problem — California actively extended the Cal Grant deadline from March 2 to June 2 in the treated year, a co-intervention specifically designed to protect aid receipt, so "no decline in aid receipt" partly measures the success of the state's mitigation rather than the harmlessness of the disruption.

The Discussion then draws a strong selection inference from these panels: declines in resubmission "were among students who were less likely to return after being enrolled, even in the absence of the policy change." That is a claim about the characteristics of marginal non-refilers, inferred from aggregate cohort means. The design cannot support it, and the paper does hedge ("Although speculative"), but the sentence is likely to be cited without the hedge.

**Measurement.** Three issues deserve a reader's attention. First, the Cal Grant on-time outcome uses the year-specific deadline — March 2 pre-policy, June 2 in the treated year. The treated cohort had a three-month-longer window to clear the same bar, so the observed on-time declines are conservative in calendar time. This is favorable to the paper's conclusions but means the outcome definition is not constant across years, and the paper does not raise it when interpreting the coefficients. Second, the family-size break (3.03 → 3.53, tax exemptions replacing self-report) makes Table 1's 2024 column non-comparable on that row; family size is also a control variable, but since all three refiling cohorts first filed pre-2024, baseline family size should be consistently measured for Tables 2–4 — the paper never states whether controls are measured at first filing or contemporaneously, and readers should assume the former and note the ambiguity. Third, the loss of individual income in 2024 (a legal consequence of the IRS data linkage) forces reliance on zip-code median household income, SNAP rates, and racial composition. The paper names the ecological-inference risk directly.

That ecological problem matters most for the paper's equity headline. Note the internal tension: freshman declines were 6–8% across all three zip INCOME terciles — no gradient at all — while the non-white-share cut shows +2% in the whitest tercile versus −8% in the least-white. The single measure producing a gradient is the one most vulnerable to ecological bias, and "non-white share" pools Asian, Black, and Hispanic populations whose college-going behavior differs sharply. The Hispanic-share disaggregation (appendix Table A7) would be more interpretable but is not in the main text. Readers who want to build on "the policy hurt students of color most" are relying on a neighborhood-level correlation reported only in the supplement.

**Inference and reporting.** SEs are clustered at the zip code, which is defensible for the covariate structure but irrelevant to the design's actual uncertainty: treatment varies at the cohort level, there is one treated cohort, and no untreated units exist. Every coefficient in Tables 2–4 carries p<.01 stars because N is roughly half a million per year, not because the counterfactual is well pinned down. Tables 2–4 report no sample sizes, no fit statistics, and no full control list ("e.g., age, dependency status, family size" and "zip-code-level socioeconomic factors"), so cell-level precision cannot be judged independently. Footnote 3's phrasing — "We select 25% of individuals from the sample so they are observed in all years" — reads ambiguously; taken literally it would suggest a balanced panel conditioned on appearing every year, which would condition on the outcome and invalidate the refiling analysis. The reported refiling rates (56–60%, i.e., most applicants do NOT appear in consecutive years) and the varying annual N (510,360 / 494,303 / 533,221 / 537,112) confirm the benign reading: individuals are sampled once by identifier so the same people are captured whenever they appear. Readers should note the ambiguity but not worry about it.

**Coverage exclusions.** Undocumented students filing the California Dream Act Application are excluded entirely (footnote 1). Mixed-status families — where a citizen student has undocumented parents lacking SSNs, the exact population blocked from electronic submission and forced into a weeks-long manual process — are in the data but unidentifiable, at an estimated ~10% of applicants. Every estimate in the paper averages over a subgroup with almost certainly much larger effects, and the paper says so ("any results, such as the lack of declines in enrollment, may not be true for all groups in California").

**Unverifiable.** The online appendix was not available for this review. Tables A1–A7 carry the summary statistics by dependency status, the submission-change estimates the Results narrate but never tabulate in the main text, the logistic propensity model, the random-forest robustness check on the terciles, the enrollment disaggregation, the school-fixed-effects robustness check backing footnote 6's claim that "these estimates are robust to different specifications," and the Hispanic-share equity result. A substantial share of load-bearing quantitative content — including the paper's most policy-salient finding — sits outside the main text.

**Bottom line for a reader.** Rely on: the descriptive submission facts (freshman filing fell, continuing-student filing rose, the composition of applicants shifted toward incumbents); the direction of the refiling decline (negative, everywhere, on both the any-refile and on-time margins); and the general point that timing disruption was concentrated at the entry margin. Treat cautiously: any specific magnitude, any distributional ranking of who was hurt most, the neighborhood-race equity gradient, and — most of all — the enrollment and aid-receipt results, which the design cannot identify and which have a live sectoral-substitution explanation the data cannot rule out.

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper covers the core administrative-burden and FAFSA-simplification literature competently and with genuine cross-disciplinary reach for a short *Educational Researcher* feature (public administration via Moynihan/Herd alongside economics of take-up via Bhargava & Manoli and Finkelstein & Notowidigdo), but the review is thin at exactly the points that matter most for its own contribution. It omits the FAFSA-renewal/refiling literature that is the direct antecedent to its headline outcome, engages almost none of the contemporaneous 2024–25 Better FAFSA evidence base despite being an "early evidence" paper accepted in May 2026, and contains at least one substantive mischaracterization (prior-prior year) and one garbled citation (the National Student Clearinghouse report) that readers should not repeat without checking the sources. Readers can trust the paper's data contribution more than they can trust its map of what was already known.

**Strengths:**

- The foundational administrative-burden framing is correctly sourced and appropriate: Moynihan, Herd & Harvey (2015) for the burden construct, Herd et al. (2013) on Medicaid simplification, Dynarski & Scott-Clayton (2006) on FAFSA complexity, and Bettinger et al. (2012) as the canonical FAFSA-assistance experiment. For a journal with a tight reference budget, the selection is economical rather than padded.
- Genuine interdisciplinary reach beyond education policy: Bhargava & Manoli (2015, *AER*) on psychological frictions in EITC take-up and Finkelstein & Notowidigdo (2019, *QJE*) on SNAP are the right cross-program anchors, and their inclusion signals that the authors understand FAFSA non-filing as an instance of a general take-up problem rather than a purely postsecondary phenomenon.
- The policy-reform sub-literature is organized around a defensible and honest arc — federal-level interventions (prior-prior year, IRS Data Retrieval Tool removal, national nudge campaigns) produced small or null effects, while state mandates (Texas, Louisiana) produced large ones — and the paper states this mixed record plainly rather than cherry-picking successes.
- Bird et al. (2021) is characterized accurately: the national nudging-at-scale campaign did produce precise nulls on FAFSA completion, aid receipt, and enrollment, and the paper does not soften this.
- The California-specific context is grounded in California-specific work (Friedmann & Martorell 2018 on Pell money left on the table), which is more than many state-based studies bother to do.
- The paper is candid in its own text about interpretive limits (the closing invitation for readers to reason about the counterfactual trend, and the acknowledgment that COVID-era recovery and the policy shock cannot be separated), which partially compensates for the thin positioning.

**Weaknesses:**

- The description of the prior-prior year reform is wrong in a way that matters. The paper states that PPY allowed students to use tax information from the prior year — but that describes the pre-reform system. The reform's defining feature is the shift to income data from two years prior (hence "prior-prior"), which is what made the October opening feasible. The error appears in the sentence introducing Bettinger, Gurantz, Lee & Long (2023), a paper on which the second author is a co-author. Readers should not repeat this sentence.
- The FAFSA renewal/refiling literature is absent, even though refiling is the paper's central regression outcome. Bird & Castleman's descriptive work on rates and patterns of FAFSA renewal (*Research in Higher Education*, 2016) and Castleman & Page's freshman-year financial aid nudge experiment on renewal and persistence (*Journal of Human Resources*, 2016) are the direct antecedents for treating refiling as a consequential margin. Their absence means the paper never establishes what normal refiling attrition looks like, which is precisely the baseline a reader needs to judge whether a 1.7–2.4 percentage-point decline is large or small.
- Almost no engagement with the contemporaneous evidence on the 2024–25 rollout itself. The rollout literature here consists of the GAO report, one NSC report, an EdSource news item, and a CSAC web page. The National College Attainment Network FAFSA Tracker — the primary real-time national source on class-of-2024 completion declines and the reference point most readers will have in mind — is not cited, nor are Federal Student Aid's own FAFSA submission and completion data releases. Given a July 2025 submission and a May 2026 acceptance, the reference list is strikingly light on 2025–2026 scholarship (only Kim 2025 and a newspaper piece).
- The National Student Clearinghouse citation is internally inconsistent and load-bearing. It is dated 2024 but titled for Spring 2025, while both places it is used in the text concern fall 2024 enrollment. More seriously, NSC publicly corrected its Fall 2024 freshman enrollment estimate in early 2025 — an initially reported freshman decline was revised to a freshman increase after a dual-enrollment misclassification was identified. The paper's framing that enrollments "surprisingly" rose rests on exactly the statistic that was revised, and the correction is never mentioned.
- The paper cites evidence that cuts against its own thesis without engaging it. Narayan (2020) is invoked to say that the sudden removal of the IRS Data Retrieval Tool had little effect — i.e., that a comparable administrative-burden shock to the FAFSA produced small behavioral responses. That finding sits in direct tension with attributing large freshman declines to the Better FAFSA transition, and the tension is never addressed.
- The administrative-burden framing is decorative rather than analytical. Moynihan et al.'s three-cost taxonomy (learning, psychological, compliance) is cited but never used, despite the paper's core finding — novice filers harmed, experienced filers unaffected or improved — being close to a textbook demonstration of learning costs. The theory is introduced and then dropped.
- There is no stated contribution relative to the closest antecedents. The contribution paragraph says only that the paper evaluates early changes from the Better FAFSA on student behavior. It never says what was already known from aggregate national trackers versus what individual-level CSAC data add, which leaves readers without a basis for deciding what to cite this paper for.
- The literature does not return in the results or discussion. The results section cites nothing; the discussion cites four items. Findings are never put back into conversation with prior work, and at least one discussion claim — that poor implementation could erode future support for government services — is an assertion from the policy-feedback literature (Soss, Mettler, Herd & Moynihan's book-length treatment) offered without any citation.
- The verification literature is engaged only through a single practitioner report (AlQaisi et al. 2020, NASFAA), despite verification being named as one of the FAFSA's core burdens and despite verification requirements changing materially under the Simplification Act. Readers looking for evidence on verification melt will need to go elsewhere.
- The Texas and Louisiana mandates are described as if equivalent. Texas requires completion of the FAFSA/TASFA or a signed opt-out form; Louisiana made it a graduation requirement. The paper's phrasing blurs a design difference that plausibly explains the different effect sizes it reports.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before repeating this paper's account of prior-prior year, read Bettinger, Gurantz, Lee & Long (2023, *Research in Higher Education*) directly. PPY moved applicants to income data from two years prior; the paper's one-sentence summary describes the pre-reform rule and should not be quoted.
- Read this paper alongside Bird & Castleman on FAFSA renewal patterns and Castleman & Page's renewal-nudge experiment. They supply the baseline attrition rates and the prior causal evidence on the refiling margin that this paper's regressions implicitly assume but never state — without them it is hard to judge whether the reported 1.7–2.7 percentage-point refiling declines are large.
- Treat the National Student Clearinghouse citation as unreliable as printed: the year, title term, and the enrollment period discussed in the text do not line up. Go to the NSC Fall 2024 Current Term Enrollment Estimates and, critically, to NSC's own correction notice revising its Fall 2024 freshman estimate. The correction bears directly on the paper's freshman-decline-but-enrollment-rose framing.
- For the national picture of the 2024–25 rollout that this paper does not provide, read the NCAN FAFSA Tracker end-of-cycle reports for the class of 2024 and Federal Student Aid's submission/completion data releases. This paper is a California microdata study, not a national account, and readers should not use it as a substitute for the national trackers.
- Verify Deneault (2023) directly before citing the 19-percentage-point Louisiana figure. The paper gives no table or page anchor, and mandate-effect magnitudes vary substantially depending on whether the outcome is completion among graduates, among seniors, or school-level completion rates.
- Read Page et al. (2023) before repeating the claim that nudges temporarily raise refiling rates. That national experiment is generally read as a null or near-null result; the paper's phrasing is more optimistic than the study's own framing, and the temporary-then-fading characterization may be importing findings from earlier smaller-scale nudge work.
- Note that Eng & Matsudaira (2021) studies outcomes among federal aid recipients; it is used here to support a claim about non-filers being less likely to persist. That is a selection-different population, so read the persistence claim as suggestive rather than sourced.
- Situate the contribution yourself, since the paper does not: the aggregate finding that freshman FAFSA filing fell in 2024–25 was already established by national trackers. What is distinctive here is individual-level California data linking refiling to Cal Grant deadline compliance, subsequent state aid receipt, and public-college reenrollment — a linkage the aggregate sources cannot make. Cite this paper for the refiling-to-outcomes linkage and the California heterogeneity, not for the existence of the freshman decline.
- Supply the theory the paper leaves on the table: Moynihan and Herd's learning-cost concept (and their 2018 book *Administrative Burden*) predicts precisely the novice-versus-veteran asymmetry this paper documents, and Herd and Moynihan's work on recertification burden is the natural frame for refiling. Reading them alongside makes the paper's findings considerably more interpretable than the paper itself makes them.
- Hold the paper's causal language loosely in light of Narayan (2020), which it cites: an earlier abrupt FAFSA burden shock produced small effects. A reader who takes Narayan seriously should ask why this shock would be so much larger, and the paper does not answer that question.
- If you need the mixed-status-family story that the paper flags as substantively important but cannot measure, look outside this reference list entirely — the paper cites only a news article and informal CSAC conversation on this point, and the qualitative and sociological literature on how immigrant and mixed-status families experience aid applications is not represented at all.

**Detailed Commentary:**

**Structure and scope.** The literature review occupies roughly two of the paper's twelve pages and is organized in four moves: FAFSA as administrative burden; prior attempts to reduce that burden; what the Simplification Act changed; and how the rollout went. That architecture is sensible, and for a short *Educational Researcher* feature the twenty-four-item reference list is defensible in size. The concerns here are not primarily about length. They are about which items are missing, whether the ones present are described accurately, and whether the review is doing analytical work or simply clearing throat before the data.

**The prior-prior year error.** The clearest problem is the sentence introducing Bettinger, Gurantz, Lee & Long (2023), which says the 2017 reform allowed students to use tax information from the prior year. That is the system PPY replaced. The reform's substance is the move to income data from two years prior, which is what made an October rather than January opening administratively possible — the paper gets the October shift right in the same sentence while getting the tax year wrong, which suggests a drafting slip rather than a misunderstanding. But it survived three rounds of revision (received July 2025, revised February and April 2026, accepted May 2026) and readers who encounter PPY here for the first time will take away a wrong definition. Flag it and go to the source.

**The missing refiling literature.** This is the most consequential omission. The paper's regression analysis is entirely about refiling, and its most-cited-in-future finding will likely be the refiling declines in Table 2 through Table 4. Yet the review contains no work on FAFSA renewal as such. Bird and Castleman's descriptive study of FAFSA renewal rates and patterns and Castleman and Page's experiment on freshman-year renewal nudges are the two studies a reader most needs in order to evaluate these estimates. Their absence has a concrete cost: because the paper never establishes what ordinary year-to-year refiling attrition or its cyclical variation looks like, the reader is given point estimates (a 1.7-percentage-point overall decline, 2.4 points for dependents, 2.7 for the high-propensity tercile) with no external yardstick. The paper's own 2023-cohort coefficients (positive, +2.2 points overall) do gesture at year-to-year volatility, and the authors honestly note that this volatility could mean they are understating the effect — but that is an internal comparison substituting for a literature the field already has.

**The absent contemporaneous evidence base.** A paper whose value proposition is early evidence on a 2024–25 policy rollout should tell readers what else the early evidence says. This one largely does not. Its rollout sources are the GAO report, a single National Student Clearinghouse release, an EdSource news article, and a CSAC web page cited in a footnote to support the claim of a rebound in the following year. The National College Attainment Network FAFSA Tracker — the source most readers, practitioners, and journalists actually used to follow the 2024 completion declines in real time — is not cited anywhere, nor are Federal Student Aid's own submission and completion data releases. This matters for how readers should place the paper: the fact that freshman FAFSA filing fell in 2024–25 was not news by the time of publication, and the paper is not the source to cite for it. What is genuinely new here is the individual-level linkage between refiling, deadline compliance, state aid receipt, and reenrollment, which aggregate trackers structurally cannot provide. The paper's own contribution statement — that it evaluates early changes from the Better FAFSA on student behavior — is too vague to convey this, so readers should do the positioning work themselves.

**The National Student Clearinghouse citation.** The reference is dated 2024 but titled for a Spring 2025 term, while both in-text uses concern fall 2024 enrollment: the introduction's claim that statistics surprisingly showed enrollments rose in fall 2024, and the results section's comparison of the paper's sector-level reenrollment gains to the nationwide NSC report. The mismatch is not merely bibliographic housekeeping. NSC's Fall 2024 freshman enrollment figure was the subject of a publicly announced correction in early 2025, in which an initially reported freshman decline was revised into a freshman increase after a dual-enrollment classification error was identified. That episode is directly relevant to a paper whose framing turns on a surprising national enrollment increase coexisting with a freshman FAFSA collapse. A reader should establish for themselves which NSC vintage supports the claim before repeating it. The correction did occur; verify its exact magnitudes at the source.

**Conflicting evidence and unused theory.** The review's own summary of federal-level interventions works against the paper's thesis and the tension goes unacknowledged. Narayan (2020) is cited for the finding that the abrupt removal of the IRS Data Retrieval Tool — an unambiguous, sudden increase in FAFSA compliance burden — had little effect. If that is true, a reader is entitled to ask why the Better FAFSA transition should produce a seven percent freshman submission decline. Plausible answers exist (the rollout combined a burden increase with a three-month timing shock, deadline chaos, and a hard block for mixed-status families), but the paper does not offer them in the literature review or the discussion. Relatedly, the administrative-burden apparatus is introduced and then never used. Moynihan, Herd and Harvey's decomposition into learning, psychological, and compliance costs would organize this paper's central result — first-time filers harmed, experienced filers stable or improved — almost perfectly, since learning costs are exactly the component that falls with prior experience. The discussion instead offers an informal speculation that continuing students feel more invested. That is a theoretical claim the cited literature could have adjudicated.

**Placement in adjacent fields.** Credit where due: for an education journal, reaching to Bhargava and Manoli in the *AER* and Finkelstein and Notowidigdo in the *QJE* is more than perfunctory, and it correctly frames FAFSA non-filing as an instance of the general take-up problem. What is thinner is the public administration side beyond the single Moynihan citation — Herd and Moynihan's book-length treatment, and their work on recertification burden in particular, is the closest conceptual analogue to annual FAFSA refiling and is absent. The discussion also makes an explicit policy-feedback claim, that poor implementation could erode future support for government services, with no citation at all; that is a live empirical literature (Soss, Mettler, and successors), not a throwaway. Finally, given that mixed-status families are treated as a substantive mechanism — estimated at perhaps ten percent of applicants, discussed in the California context section and in the notes — the complete absence of qualitative or sociological work on how immigrant and mixed-status families navigate aid applications is a notable gap in an interdisciplinary journal.

**Limits of this assessment.** Knowledge of the 2024–2026 Better FAFSA literature is bounded, and it cannot be ruled out that relevant academic work published in late 2025 or 2026 either did not exist at submission or is genuinely thin — the rollout is recent and microdata access is scarce, which is part of what makes this paper useful. Confidence is high regarding the prior-prior year error, the absence of the FAFSA renewal literature, the internal inconsistency of the NSC citation, and the unengaged tension with Narayan (2020), since all four are verifiable from the paper's own text against well-established sources. Confidence is lower on the exact magnitude reported for Deneault (2023) and on the precise characterization of Page et al. (2023), which is why both are flagged as items to verify rather than as errors.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper is clearly written, conventionally organized, and accessible to a general *Educational Researcher* audience, and most of its numeric claims check out against Tables 1–4. But a careful reader will hit several genuine traps that survived production: one paragraph of Table 3 statistics that does not match the table at all, a freshman refiling sentence that pairs the freshman coefficient with the all-applicant baseline, a cohort-labeling scheme that changes three times within two pages, and an abstract that drops the conditioning that makes its most reassuring finding interpretable. Read the tables, not the prose, whenever a specific number matters.

**Strengths:**

- Conventional, navigable architecture (Intro, Literature Review in three labeled subsections, California Context, Data, Methods, four Results subsections, Discussion). A reader can find any component quickly, and the California Context section front-loads exactly the institutional detail (Cal Grant value, March 2 deadline extended to June 2, Dream Act applications excluded) needed to read the results.
- The implementation-failure narrative on page 3 is the most valuable expository passage in the paper: it is concrete, sourced to the GAO report, and gives the reader a mechanism (mixed-status families blocked from electronic submission, unanswered calls, late corrections) that makes the freshman/first-time-filer pattern legible rather than merely statistical.
- Prose is plain and jargon-light, with explicit signposting of the two analyses (descriptive submission trends, then cohort-comparison refiling regressions) in the introduction and again in Methods.
- Considerable methodological candor is expressed in prose: the loss of individual family income, the ecological-bias warning about zip-code proxies, the explicit statement that the study cannot observe outcomes for new (non-refiling) students, and the closing invitation for readers to form their own counterfactual. The paper also states its policy of rounding percent changes to whole numbers to avoid overstating precision.
- Most verifiable numbers are correct. Table 1 descriptives, the Table 2 dependency-status arithmetic, the Table 2 Cal Grant education-level figures, the Table 3 FAFSA-refiling terciles, and every Table 4 number checked reproduce exactly. Footnote 5's headcount decomposition also reconciles with the 25% sample Ns.

**Weaknesses:**

- A whole paragraph of Table 3 statistics contradicts Table 3. The text reports Cal Grant refiling declines of 2.9 pp (8%) for the middle tercile, 1.1 pp (4%) for the lowest, and 2.0 pp (4%) for the highest. Table 3's 2024 Cohort (Cal Grant) row gives −.020 (middle), −.001 and statistically insignificant (low), and −.027 (high). None of the three text figures appears in the table, and no permutation or differencing of table values produces them. Most consequentially, the text describes a 4% decline for the lowest-propensity group where the table shows essentially zero and the only unstarred estimate in the panel.
- Baseline mix-up in the headline refiling sentence. The text says the freshman refile rate fell 1.7 pp from a 57.7% baseline to 56.0%. Table 2 Panel A shows .577 is the ALL column baseline; the freshman baseline is .531, so the freshman path is .531 − .017 = .514, not 56.0%. The arithmetic in the sentence is the all-applicant arithmetic wearing a freshman label. (The paper gets the analogous Cal Grant sentence right, using the correct 32.9% freshman baseline, which makes this a slip rather than a systematic misreading.)
- Three incompatible cohort-labeling conventions, sometimes within one paragraph. Methods defines cohorts by refiling year (2022, 2023, 2024) and Tables 2–4 use those labels; the equation description instead labels by first-file year (2021, 2022, 2023); and the dependency-status paragraph switches again to calendar years that match neither. That paragraph puts the .657 dependent baseline in 2024 and the .633 endpoint in 2025, when .657 is the 2022 cohort's rate, two cohorts earlier. The same paragraph then reverts to table labels for the independent Cal Grant null. A reader cannot carry one mental model through the section.
- The identification check stated in Methods fails in every table, and the reader is not warned at the point of use. Methods says the pre-period coefficient should be near zero; it is instead large and significant everywhere (+.022 all, +.028 freshmen, +.034 independent, +.037 lowest tercile). The paper acknowledges the rising pre-trend a page later and reinterprets it as making declines understated, but never retracts the stated expectation. The practical consequence for readers is that every reported decline is measured against a baseline two cohorts back during a rising trend, so declines relative to the immediately preceding cohort are roughly double. The paper performs that differencing exactly once (Table 3, the 3.3 to 4.3 pp range, which does reproduce) and nowhere else, so magnitudes are not comparable across paragraphs.
- The abstract drops the conditioning that governs its most reassuring claim. It reports higher rates of state aid receipt and public college enrollment without noting that Table 4 Panel B is restricted to students who already received state aid the prior year and Panel C to students already enrolled in a California public college. Methods and Results both disclose this; the abstract does not, and the Discussion only loosens it to refiling students. Readers who stop at the abstract will take a conditional-on-prior-receipt result as a population statement.
- A misplaced paragraph interrupts the Table 2 discussion. The appendix Table A7 paragraph on Hispanic-share zip codes sits inside the refiling section but reports percent changes in applications, i.e., it belongs with the earlier submissions subsection. It also introduces a second neighborhood race cut (Hispanic share) that partially duplicates and partially conflicts with the non-white-share terciles reported earlier, in a different section, with no bridge between them.
- Minimizing language around the number that most complicates the paper's story. The observation that 2024 freshman submissions exceeded 2021 and 2022 is qualified as "slightly higher." Reconstructed from Table 1 (share times N), 2024 freshman submissions run about 7.5% above 2021 and 8.7% above 2022; even under worst-case rounding of the two-decimal shares the gap is at least ~3%. Relatedly, the page 2 summary paragraph describes freshman applications falling sharply and never mentions the overall ~1% increase, so a reader who stops after the introduction gets a more negative picture than the abstract or the results support.
- The Discussion's central rhetorical claim outruns the exhibits and is contradicted by the paper's own Table 3. The assertion that the policy harmed families already facing the steepest barriers rests entirely on the zip-code non-white-share cut; the income-tercile cut showed uniform 6–8% freshman declines with no gradient, and Table 3 shows the lowest refiling-propensity tercile declined least (0.6 pp, ~1%) while the highest declined most (2.7 pp). Two paragraphs later the Discussion advances the opposite reading, that decliners were students unlikely to return anyway. Neither tension is reconciled.
- Half the analysis is not in the article. The entire submissions section carries no numeric in-article exhibit: Figures 1 and 2 are cumulative line charts, and every disaggregated percent change is sourced to online appendix Table A2, cited three times. Appendix Tables A1, A3, A4, A5, A6, and A7 carry the summary statistics by dependency, the propensity model, the random-forest alternative, enrollment by dependency, and the school-fixed-effects robustness. Tables 2–4 also report no sample sizes, so the conditional Panels B and C of Table 4 have unknown denominators.
- Smaller consistency lapses: the cycle length is given as 19 months when the stated window (October 1 through June 30 of the following academic year) is 21; sectors are defined as CC in Data but appear as CCC in Results and Table 4 and as CA community colleges in Table 1; the upper-division category is called Junior & senior, Other, and upper-division in three places; Table 1 enrollment is described as rising steadily from 48% to 51% when the series dips to 47% in 2023; and the claim that the largest sector increase was in community colleges is a tie at two decimals (CSU and CCC both +2 points, with CSU's 2024 figure merely restoring its 2021–22 level after a 2023 dip).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Table 2 Panel A and Table 4 are the load-bearing exhibits and both reproduce cleanly; anchor your reading there. Table 4 in particular is the paper's most trustworthy page: every text claim checked against it (2 pp / ~3% refiling declines across sectors, CCC Cal Grant 43.3% to 40.5% for 6%, UC's decline already present in the prior cohort, CSU's Cal Grant null, CSU reenrollment 57.1% to 61.9% for 8%, UC and CCC +1.9 pp) is correct.
- Do not quote the Table 3 Cal Grant sentence. Its three figures (2.9/1.1/2.0 pp and 8%/4%/4%) do not appear in Table 3, which shows −.020, −.001 (not significant), and −.027. The qualitative ranking (middle tercile largest in relative terms) survives; the magnitudes do not. If you want the lowest-tercile result, the honest statement is that there was no detectable change in on-time refiling for that group.
- Do not quote the freshman refiling sentence's 57.7% to 56.0% path. Substitute the freshman baseline from Table 2 Panel A: .531 to .514. Use the Cal Grant version of the freshman result (1.9 pp off a 32.9% base, ~6%) if you need one number, because that one is stated correctly.
- Before reading Tables 2–4, fix the cohort convention in your head from the Methods paragraph: the 2022, 2023, and 2024 cohorts are students who first filed in 2021, 2022, and 2023 and refiled for 2022–23, 2023–24, and 2024–25. Then ignore every calendar year printed in the dependency-status paragraph. Its arithmetic is right (.489 + .034 = .523, .489 − .011 = .478, .657 − .024 = .633) but the years attached to those numbers are not.
- For any decline in Tables 2–4, compute both differences yourself: the reported coefficient (versus the two-cohorts-back baseline) and the coefficient minus the 2023-cohort coefficient (versus the immediately prior cohort). The pre-trend is positive and significant throughout, so the two answers differ by a factor of roughly two, and the paper reports the second one only for Table 3. This single habit resolves most of the apparent inconsistency between paragraphs.
- Read the Data section in full; it is short and it is where the binding limitations live (no individual income after 2024, no individual race or ethnicity, zip-code proxies, mixed-status families unidentified). The Discussion's neighborhood-composition claims are only interpretable with that section in hand.
- Treat the submissions half of the Results as a pointer to material you cannot see. Every percentage in it comes from online appendix Table A2, and the Hispanic-share result comes from Table A7. If you need those numbers, fetch the supplement; the figures alone will not let you check them.
- You can skim the first Literature Review subsection and the Simplification Act description if you already know the policy; the implementation subsection on page 3 is the one to actually read. The Discussion's final two paragraphs of policy recommendations (auto-renewal, college-level FAFSA mandates) are generic and can be skimmed.
- Read the abstract's last sentence as conditional. Higher state aid receipt and enrollment are estimated only among students who already received state aid, or were already enrolled in a California public college, the prior year, and only within the three public systems. The paper says so twice in the body but not in the abstract.
- Treat the causal framing as the paper's weakest seam and read Methods and Discussion together. Methods says the key coefficient isolates the policy change; the Discussion says the study is descriptive and invites readers to construct their own counterfactual. The Discussion's framing is the defensible one.

**Detailed Commentary:**

**Organization and navigability.** The paper follows the standard quantitative template and does it well. Section headers are informative rather than generic (the Results subsections name their content: total submissions, submissions by the state aid deadline, refiling behavior, and refiling/aid/enrollment by sector). The California Context section is a genuine service to the reader, establishing the Cal Grant's magnitude (\$6,500 CSU, \$17,000 UC, ~\$1,600 community college) against the \$7,395 maximum Pell before any results appear, so the stakes of the on-time-filing outcome are clear when it arrives. At twelve pages the paper is appropriately sized for its evidence. The main navigability failure is the appendix dependency: the first Results section, roughly a third of the empirical content, contains no in-article numeric exhibit and refers the reader to online Table A2 three separate times, with Table A7 supplying the Hispanic-share cut. A reader working from the article alone can verify the refiling analysis and essentially none of the submissions analysis.

A second, smaller navigability problem is the stray paragraph. Inside the refiling section, between the Table 2 education-level discussion and the Cal Grant refiling discussion, sits a paragraph about Hispanic-share zip codes that reports percent changes in applications (a 10% increase in overall applications and 11% among freshmen in the lowest-Hispanic-share zips; roughly no change overall and an 8% freshman decline in the highest). That is submissions content, in the submissions vocabulary, parked in the refiling section, and the following paragraph resumes the Table 2 thread as if it had not been interrupted. It also creates a duplicate-but-different neighborhood race analysis: the earlier submissions section reported non-white-share terciles (freshmen up ~2% in the whitest zips, down 8% in the least-white), while this paragraph reports Hispanic-share terciles (+11% and −8% for freshmen). The two cuts overlap without being the same, they live in different sections, and the paper never relates them.

**Text versus table audit.** Tables 1–4 were reconstructed from the linearized extraction and every numeric claim in the Results checked. Here is the complete ledger.

*Confirmed correct.* Table 1: refiler share .60/.57/.56 for 2022–2024 matches the text; independent share 46–48%; freshman shares .47/.48/.52/.48; family size 3.04/3.06/3.03 versus 3.53; income unavailable in 2024. Text on total submissions: the 2024 total is 537,112 against 533,221 in 2023, a 0.73% increase, correctly described as just under 1%. Freshman submissions reconstructed as share times N fall from 277,275 to 257,814, exactly −7.0%, correctly described as almost 7%. Footnote 5's decomposition reconciles: the total change scaled by four is about 15,600 (stated ~16,000), the freshman change about −77,800 (stated 73,000 fewer), and the non-freshman change about +93,400 (stated 87,000) — the last two are looser but within what two-decimal share rounding permits. Table 2 Panel A Cal Grant: the 2023-cohort range of −0.2 to 1.2 pp across education levels matches (.007 all, .012 freshman, −.002 sophomore, .004 other); the freshman on-time decline of 1.9 pp off a 32.9% base is 5.8%, correctly rounded to 6%; the sophomore −1.9 pp and junior/senior −0.5 pp match exactly. Table 2 Panel B: dependent .657 − .024 = .633, and .024/.657 = 3.7%, correctly rounded to 4%; independent .489 + .034 = .523 and .489 − .011 = .478; the independent Cal Grant null is indeed −.000; dependent on-time −.026 off .466 is 5.6%, correctly rounded to 6%. Table 3 FAFSA panel: middle −.024 off .588 is 4.1% and high −.027 off .737 is 3.7%, both correctly given as 4%; low −.006 off .480 is 1.25%, correctly given as about 1%; the versus-prior-cohort differences are −.043 (low), −.042 (middle), −.033 (high), exactly the stated 3.3 to 4.3 pp range. Table 4: sector refiling declines of −.023/−.020/−.022 off .729/.716/.687 are 3.2%/2.8%/3.2%, correctly summarized as just over two points or approximately 3%; CCC Cal Grant .433 − .028 = .405 and 6.5%, given as 6%; UC's −.025 in 2024 against −.026 in 2023, correctly described as mostly present already; CSU's Cal Grant coefficients (−.004, +.003, both insignificant) support the no-change claim; CSU reenrollment .571 + .048 = .619 and 8.4%, given as 8%; UC and CCC reenrollment both +.019, being 3.0% and 3.7% off .625 and .508, given as approximately 3% to 4%.

*Confirmed mismatches.* (1) Table 3, Cal Grant terciles. The text gives declines of 2.9 pp (8%) middle, 1.1 pp (4%) lowest, 2.0 pp (4%) highest. Table 3's 2024 Cohort (Cal Grant) row is −.001 (low, no stars), −.020 (middle), −.027 (high), with baselines .261, .366, .563, implying relative declines of 0.4%, 5.5%, and 4.8%. The text's pp and % figures are internally consistent with each other (1.1/.261 = 4.2%, 2.9/.366 = 7.9%, 2.0/.563 = 3.6%), which is the signature of a paragraph left over from an earlier version of the table rather than a transcription slip. Differencing against the 2023 cohort does not recover them either (−.024, −.027, −.016). The ordinal claim that the middle tercile shows the largest relative decline does survive in the table; the magnitudes and, critically, the significance of the lowest-tercile result do not. (2) Table 2 Panel A, freshman refiling. The text's 57.7% baseline is the All column; the freshman baseline is .531. The stated 1.7 pp decline is the correct freshman coefficient, but 57.7 − 1.7 = 56.0 is all-applicant arithmetic. (3) Table 1, sector enrollment. The claim that the largest 2024 increase was in community colleges is a tie at the reported precision (CSU .11 to .13, CCC .32 to .34), and CSU's move merely restores its 2021–22 level of .13 after a 2023 dip. (4) Table 1, overall enrollment. Described as rising steadily from 48% to 51%, but the series is .48, .49, .47, .51, i.e., non-monotone. (5) The freshman-versus-2021-and-2022 comparison. Reconstructed counts put 2024 about 7.5% above 2021 and 8.7% above 2022; the floor under worst-case rounding is roughly 3%. "Slightly higher" is not a fair description of that gap, and this is the one comparison in the paper that most complicates the freshman-collapse narrative.

*Non-numeric errors and inconsistencies.* The Methods section states the application cycle ends 19 months after October 1; the Results section's own example (October 1, 2022 through June 30, 2024) is 21 months, and 21 is the correct span for the window described. Since Figures 1 and 2 plot cumulative submissions across exactly this window and the reader gets only captions, the misstatement directly affects how the figures are read. Sector nomenclature shifts from CC (Data) to CCC (Results, Table 4) to CA community colleges (Table 1). The upper-division category is Junior & senior in Table 1, Other in Table 2, and upper-division or juniors and seniors in the text. Tables 2, 3, and 4 share an identical note that lists dependency status among the controls, which sits awkwardly with Table 2 Panel B splitting the sample by dependency status. No table reports sample sizes, which matters most for Table 4 Panels B and C, whose samples are restricted to prior state aid recipients and prior public-college enrollees respectively and whose sizes are therefore unknowable from the article.
