**Cohort labeling.** This deserves separate treatment because it is the single largest comprehension obstacle. Three conventions coexist. Methods and Tables 2–4 label by refiling year: the 2022, 2023, and 2024 cohorts first filed in 2021, 2022, and 2023. The equation's prose description labels by first-filing year, defining dummies for 2022 and 2023 relative to 2021. The dependency-status paragraph uses calendar years that match neither, placing the .657 dependent baseline in 2024 and the .633 endpoint in 2025, when .657 is the 2022 cohort. The freshman paragraph and the pre-trend caveat both invoke a 2021 cohort that does not exist in any table. Within the single dependency paragraph, the reader is handed calendar-year framing for the dependent and independent results and then table-cohort framing for the independent Cal Grant null. The arithmetic throughout that paragraph is right; only the labels are wrong. But a reader tracking levels through time will construct a false timeline, and specifically will believe the comparison is year-over-year when it is two cohorts wide.

That width is itself under-communicated. The prose describing independent students moves from 48.9% up to 52.3% and then says the rate dropped to 47.8%, which reads as a 4.5 pp collapse; the estimate the table reports is −1.1 pp against the two-years-back baseline. Both are derivable, both are meaningful, and the paper does not tell the reader which one it is asserting.

**Fidelity of argument.** The Methods section states that the pre-period coefficient should be near zero if the design is credible. It is not near zero anywhere: +.022 overall, +.028 for freshmen, +.034 for independent students, +.037 for the lowest propensity tercile, all significant at the 1% level. The paper notices this a page later and converts it into an argument that the estimated declines understate the true effect. That reinterpretation is reasonable and honestly flagged as speculative, but the stated diagnostic is never withdrawn, and a reader who takes the Methods section at face value will over-trust the design. The paper also oscillates between describing the key coefficient as isolating the policy effect and describing the study as purely descriptive; the latter is the defensible characterization and is the one the Discussion adopts.

The Discussion's most quotable sentence, that the policy harmed families already facing the steepest barriers, is the clearest case of rhetoric outrunning evidence. Its support is one cut of one proxy: freshman submissions in the least-white zip codes fell 8% versus a ~2% rise in the whitest. The income-tercile cut, reported one paragraph earlier, showed uniform 6–8% freshman declines with no gradient, which is at best neutral for the claim. And Table 3, the paper's most direct attempt to index student vulnerability, points the other way: the lowest refiling-propensity tercile declined least (0.6 pp, ~1%, and essentially zero on the Cal Grant outcome) while the highest declined most (2.7 pp). Floor effects are a plausible reconciliation, but the paper offers none, and two paragraphs later it advances the opposite interpretation, that decliners were students unlikely to have returned anyway. Both readings sit in the same section without acknowledgment that they conflict. Elsewhere the Discussion attributes the submission increase to the reforms in causal language the design does not license.

**Abstract fidelity.** The abstract is accurate on design (it says "descriptively examine" and does not claim causal identification) and accurate on the headline pattern (modest overall increase, large freshman declines, many missing the state aid deadline). Two things a reader should supply. First, the conditioning: higher aid receipt and enrollment are estimated only among students who already received state aid or were already enrolled in a public California college, within the three public systems only. The abstract states this as an unconditional observation. The Discussion improves on it slightly by saying "for refiling students," which is still looser than the actual restriction. Second, the deadline: the March 2 Cal Grant deadline was extended to June 2 in the Better FAFSA year, so failing to meet the deadline in the abstract refers to an already-extended deadline. Both facts are disclosed in the body; neither is in the abstract, and both change how the abstract's claims should be quoted. The introduction has a related framing problem in the opposite direction: its page 2 summary of findings omits the overall submission increase entirely, so the introduction reads more uniformly negative than the abstract or the results.

**Exhibits.** Table 1 is well constructed and self-contained, with a note that correctly explains the refiler variable and the missing 2024 income. Tables 2–4 are readable and consistently formatted, but three things limit them: no sample sizes anywhere, a generic shared note that does not distinguish which variables are controls versus splits, and the absence of any row reporting the 2024-versus-2023 cohort difference that the text sometimes discusses and readers repeatedly need. Figures 1 and 2 come to the reader as captions only in extracted form; even in the published article they are cumulative count charts carrying no disaggregated percentages, so the entire submissions analysis rests on an appendix table.

**What this means for trust.** The failure rate is not catastrophic. Of roughly thirty checkable numeric claims, about twenty-five reproduce exactly, including all of Table 4 and all of the Table 2 dependency and Cal Grant arithmetic. But the failures are concentrated in ways that matter: one full paragraph of Table 3 statistics is wrong, and the sentence a reader is most likely to quote about freshmen pairs the right coefficient with the wrong baseline. Combined with the labeling churn and the two-cohort comparison width, the practical rule for readers is that the qualitative story (freshmen down, continuing students up, refiling down modestly across the board, reenrollment and aid receipt up among prior recipients) is well supported, while any specific figure should be re-derived from the table before it is quoted.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This paper provides the first individual-level administrative-data portrait of the 2024–25 Better FAFSA rollout in a single large state, and its distinctive value is on the continuing-student margin — refiling behavior linked to state aid receipt and public-college reenrollment — which aggregate national trackers (NCAN, FSA, NSC) cannot observe at all. The entry-level findings (overall submissions roughly flat, freshman submissions down ~7% and ~13% by the state aid deadline) largely corroborate what public trackers already showed, while the refiling analysis contributes a genuinely new and somewhat counterintuitive fact: refiling fell modestly and uniformly, yet state aid receipt and reenrollment rose. The contribution is real but bounded, and the paper's two most quotable sentences — that students may be "enrolling, but without the support of state or federal financial aid" and that the policy "negatively impacted families that already faced the steepest barriers" — outrun what the data can show.

**Strengths:**

- Genuinely new data on a question that was, at the time of writing, covered almost entirely by aggregate counts. A 25% random sample of CSAC FAFSA applications across four cycles (~500K observations per year) with individual identifiers permits a freshman-versus-continuing decomposition, a dependency-status split, and a longitudinal refiling analysis — none of which the NCAN completion tracker or FSA application counts can support.
- The refiling-cohort design is the paper's real analytic contribution. Comparing students who first filed in 2021, 2022, and 2023 (and therefore first refiled in 2022–23, 2023–24, and the post-policy 2024–25) holds constant the fact that everyone entered the system under the old form, which is a cleaner comparison than a raw year-over-year submission count and rules out compositional change in who first enters.
- Linkage to downstream outcomes — state aid payment and public-sector reenrollment — rather than stopping at application counts. This is what turns a filing-statistics paper into one that can speak, at least partially, to whether the filing disruption mattered for students.
- The freshman/continuing divergence is the single most useful fact in the paper and is robust to how it is cut: freshmen down ~7% overall and ~13% by the state deadline, sophomores up 13–14%, upper-division up 5–6%. Because the aggregate change was under 1%, this decomposition materially corrects the reassuring national headline that FAFSA volume held up.
- Unusually candid about the design's limits. The authors explicitly note the 2023-cohort pre-period coefficient is not zero (+2.2 pp for refiling), state that this cuts against the identifying assumption in a known direction, decline to emphasize point estimates, flag ecological bias in the zip-code proxies, and — in a rare move — tell readers to form their own counterfactual. Footnote 8 pointing to the 2025–26 rebound is included even though it deflates the paper's own alarm.
- Well-scoped policy framing. The institutional detail on the Cal Grant deadline (March 2, extended to June 2), the mixed-status/SSN failure mode, and the CSAC operational account gives readers a mechanism story rather than just a time series.

**Weaknesses:**

- The abstract's inference — "many students may be enrolling, but without the support of state or federal financial aid" — is not observed anywhere in the paper. There is no Pell or federal aid receipt outcome despite a title about federal aid applications; there is no private or out-of-state enrollment; and there is no enrollment outcome at all for the freshmen whose submissions fell. A 7% drop in freshman filings is equally consistent with those students not enrolling, enrolling with aid via a late federal filing, or (in California specifically) filing a CDAA that is excluded from the data. The bridge from "fewer applications" to "enrolling without aid" is asserted, not estimated.
- The claim that "the policy appears to have negatively impacted families that already faced the steepest barriers" rests on one proxy — zip-code non-white share — and the paper's own results partly undercut it. Freshman declines were 6–8% uniformly across all three zip income terciles and SNAP terciles, so the socioeconomic-gradient story does not appear; the entire differential lives in the racial-composition proxy, which the authors concede is subject to ecological bias, and the mechanism they invoke (mixed-status families, ~10% of applicants) is never observed.
- The refiling analysis is a cohort-adjusted before/after, not a difference-in-differences — there is no untreated group in the treated year. The pre-period coefficient the design assumes is zero is instead large and positive (2023 cohort: +2.2 pp overall, +2.8 pp for freshmen), so the true policy effect could plausibly be anywhere from roughly −1.7 to −4 pp. The paper says this, but readers quoting "refiling fell 1.7 percentage points" as an effect will be treating a bounded range as a point estimate.
- The paper's interpretation of its most interesting result — that refiling declines were concentrated among students "unlikely to have continued their enrollment regardless" — is one of several live explanations and is not tested. The comparison is across panels with different conditioning sets (Panel A is all refilers; Panel B conditions on prior-year aid receipt; Panel C on prior-year public enrollment), so the composition differs and the inference does not follow cleanly. Competing readings: the June 2 deadline extension plus CSAC's aid-administration flexibility mechanically insulated payments; the reenrollment gains reflect the same post-COVID recovery visible in the NSC national data rather than anything about non-refilers; or students reenrolled while their aid packaging simply moved later in the year. The CSU reenrollment series makes this vivid — −3.1 pp for the 2023 cohort and +4.8 pp for the 2024 cohort, an 8-point swing across adjacent cohorts — which is hard to attribute to a filing policy and signals that year-to-year shocks in these outcomes are large.
- The disaggregations that carry the headline equity claim are in an online appendix (Table A2), not the main text. No main-text table reports the zip-code results at all, which is a substantial constraint for a reader trying to weigh the paper's most-quoted sentence.
- Two subgroup figures in the text are difficult to reconcile without the appendix: the results section reports freshman submissions up ~2% in the least-non-white zip codes, while the refiling section reports (from Table A7) an 11% freshman increase in the lowest-Hispanic-share zips. These are near-identical cuts of the same population producing very different magnitudes, and the second appears in a section otherwise about refiling.
- Baseline numbers are loosely labeled in the prose in ways that will propagate into citations. The text describes the freshman refile rate as falling "from a baseline of 57.7% to 56.0%," but Table 2 shows .577 is the All-students baseline and the freshman baseline is .531. Similarly, the dependent-student result is narrated as a fall "from 65.7% in 2024 to 63.3% in 2025," when .657 is the 2022-cohort baseline and the contrast is regression-adjusted, not a raw year-over-year change.
- The college-level mandatory-FAFSA recommendation does not follow from the evidence and sits in tension with the paper's own interpretation. The supporting citations (Kofoed 2017; Deneault 2023) concern high school mandates, and if the non-refilers were largely students who were not returning anyway — as the paper argues — then compelling them to file would recover little. No estimate of forgone aid dollars is offered.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Cite it for: the freshman-versus-continuing-student decomposition of the Better FAFSA year. That aggregate California FAFSA submissions rose ~1% while freshman submissions fell ~7% (~13% by the state aid deadline) and sophomore/upper-division submissions rose 13–14%/5–6% is well documented and is the paper's most durable and most useful fact — particularly as a corrective to the reassuring national headline count.
- Cite it for: evidence that the rollout disrupted continuing students, not only first-time filers. Refiling fell roughly 1.7–2.4 pp (3–4%) across education levels, dependency statuses, and all three public sectors — a broad, consistent pattern that no aggregate tracker could have detected and that is new to the literature.
- Cite it for: the descriptive fact that, among students already receiving state aid or enrolled in a California public college, state aid receipt and reenrollment did not fall in the Better FAFSA year and modestly rose. Report this as a fact about outcomes, not as evidence that the disruption was harmless.
- Cite it for: a documented case of implementation failure undermining a well-theorized simplification reform — the paper's cleanest conceptual contribution to the administrative-burden literature, and the framing the discussion supports best.
- Do not lean on it for: "students enrolled without financial aid." The data contain no federal aid or Pell receipt outcome, no private or out-of-state enrollment, and no enrollment measure at all for the freshmen whose filings fell — so the abstract's most quotable sentence is an inference from a missing-applications count, not a finding.
- Do not lean on it for: "Better FAFSA harmed the most disadvantaged families." The socioeconomic gradient is essentially absent (freshman declines were 6–8% across every income tercile); the differential appears only in a zip-code racial-composition proxy that the authors themselves flag for ecological bias, and the mixed-status mechanism is never observed.
- Do not lean on it for: causal magnitudes of the refiling effect. The design has no untreated comparison group in the treated year, and the pre-period coefficient the design assumes is zero is instead +2.2 pp — so the reported −1.7 pp is a floor under one reading and an overstatement under another. Cite the direction and rough scale, not the point estimate.
- Do not lean on it for: "the students who stopped refiling were not coming back anyway." This reading is offered by the authors as speculation, rests on comparing panels with different conditioning samples, and competes with at least two other explanations (the June 2 deadline extension and CSAC's mitigation efforts insulating aid payments; broad post-COVID enrollment recovery driving the reenrollment gains).
- Do not lean on it for: California as a representative case. If anything the state is a favorable one — the state aid deadline was extended by three months, Cal Grant generosity gives unusually strong refiling incentives, CSAC ran an active mitigation effort, and undocumented students (via the CDAA) are excluded from the data entirely. National or lower-capacity-state effects are plausibly worse, which makes California's estimates closer to a lower bound than an average.
- Open question a reader should know remains unresolved: federal aid receipt. Despite the title, no Pell or federal disbursement outcome is observed, so whether the filing decline translated into lost federal aid — the mechanism through which harm would actually operate — is untested.
- Open question: what happened to the missing freshmen. Roughly 73,000 fewer first-time applicants (footnote 5) are unaccounted for; the data cannot distinguish non-enrollment, private/out-of-state enrollment, CDAA filing, or late unaided enrollment.
- Open question: whether this was a transitional shock or a scarring one. Footnote 8 reports a strong 2025–26 rebound in California applications, which suggests one bad year rather than a persistent break — but persistence, credit accumulation, debt, and completion for the affected 2024–25 cohorts remain unobserved and are the outcomes that would determine whether the episode mattered.
- Practical note for anyone quoting numbers from the prose: verify against Tables 2–4. Several baselines in the text are attached to the wrong column (e.g., the freshman refile baseline is .531, not the .577 stated), and some regression-adjusted contrasts are narrated as raw year-over-year changes.

**Detailed Commentary:**

**What is genuinely new versus what confirms existing knowledge.** By the time this paper appeared, the broad contour of the 2024–25 Better FAFSA rollout was public: FSA's application counts and NCAN's high-school-senior completion tracker had both documented a delayed, depressed cycle for new filers, and the National Student Clearinghouse had reported that fall 2024 enrollment nevertheless rose. On the entry margin, then, this paper largely corroborates rather than discovers — a 7% freshman decline in California is the state-level instantiation of a pattern already visible nationally.

The contribution lies elsewhere, and it is real. Aggregate trackers count applications; they cannot follow a person. With a 25% random sample of CSAC applications spanning 2021–22 through 2024–25, the authors can identify who refiled, whether they refiled by the state aid deadline, whether they subsequently received a Cal Grant payment, and whether they reenrolled in a California public institution. That combination — individual longitudinal filing behavior linked to realized aid and enrollment — was not otherwise available for the Better FAFSA year, and it opens a margin (continuing students) that the public discourse had almost entirely ignored in favor of high school seniors. The refiling-cohort construction is a sensible piece of design work: by restricting to students who first entered under the old form and comparing the cohort whose first refiling fell in 2024–25 to the two prior cohorts, it removes the compositional confound that plagues raw year-over-year comparisons.

**Significance of the two headline results.** The freshman/continuing divergence is the paper's most citable finding and is significant precisely because the aggregate masked it. A reader who saw only "California FAFSA submissions rose 1%" would draw the wrong conclusion; the decomposition (roughly 73,000 fewer first-time applicants offset by 87,000 additional continuing filers, per footnote 5) is the kind of fact that changes how a policy audience reads a national statistic. Its policy weight is amplified by the state-deadline result: the freshman decline widens from 7% to 13% when the outcome is filing by the Cal Grant deadline, which is the margin that determines eligibility for a benefit worth roughly \$6,500–\$17,000 a year. That is a substantively meaningful, well-measured finding.

The second result — refiling fell but aid receipt and reenrollment rose — is the more intellectually interesting one and the more fragile. The authors read it as evidence that the students who dropped out of the filing system were marginal students who would not have returned regardless. That is a plausible reading, but it is one of several, and the paper does not adjudicate among them. First, the panels condition on different samples: refiling is estimated on all refilers, aid receipt on prior-year aid recipients, reenrollment on prior-year public enrollees. Comparing coefficients across differently-conditioned samples cannot establish that the non-refilers in Panel A are the non-returners absent from Panels B and C. Second, California extended its state aid deadline from March 2 to June 2 specifically to absorb the rollout chaos, and CSAC ran an active mitigation effort that the authors themselves describe — both of which would mechanically protect aid receipt even if filing behavior was genuinely disrupted. Third, the reenrollment gains coincide with a national post-COVID enrollment recovery the paper cites approvingly elsewhere; attributing them to anything about non-refilers requires ruling out the secular trend, which the design cannot do. The volatility in Table 4, Panel C is the clearest warning: CSU reenrollment moves −3.1 pp for the 2023 cohort and +4.8 pp for the 2024 cohort, an eight-point swing between adjacent cohorts that no filing policy explains. If year effects of that size are routine in these outcomes, then the reassuring reading of Panels B and C is not well identified, and neither, symmetrically, is the alarming reading of Panel A.

**The gap between quotable and supported.** Two sentences will do most of this paper's citational work, and both run ahead of the evidence. The abstract's "this suggests many students may be enrolling, but without the support of state or federal financial aid" is doubly unsupported: the paper observes no federal aid receipt whatsoever — a striking omission for an article titled around federal aid applications — and observes no enrollment at all for the freshmen in question, since the enrollment analysis is restricted to prior-year enrollees. What the data show is that fewer freshmen filed. Whether those students enrolled unaided, enrolled with late federal aid, filed a California Dream Act Application (excluded from the data), enrolled privately or out of state (unobserved), or did not enroll is entirely open. The discussion's "the policy appears to have negatively impacted families that already faced the steepest barriers to financial aid access" fares somewhat better but is still thinner than it sounds: freshman declines were essentially flat at 6–8% across every zip income tercile, so the socioeconomic gradient the sentence implies does not appear in the data. The entire differential is in the racial-composition proxy — roughly +2% in the whitest zips versus −8% in the least-white zips — measured at the zip level, with the authors correctly flagging ecological bias, and with the natural mechanism (mixed-status families unable to submit without parental SSNs) invoked but never observed. The direction is credible and the mechanism is plausible; the strength of the claim is not.

A practical complication for readers: the disaggregations underwriting that equity claim live in online appendix Table A2, with no main-text table reporting them. In a twelve-page short-format article, that is a defensible editorial choice, but it means the most-quoted claim is the least verifiable from the article itself. Two figures in the text are also hard to square without the appendix — a ~2% freshman increase in the least-non-white zips in one place, an 11% freshman increase in the lowest-Hispanic-share zips in another — and the prose repeatedly attaches the All-column baseline to subgroup coefficients (the freshman refile baseline is .531 in Table 2, not the .577 the text states) and narrates regression-adjusted contrasts as if they were raw year-over-year changes. None of this is fatal, but anyone extracting numbers should work from the tables.

**Generalizability.** The paper is honest about California being one state and lists the usual caveats, but it underplays the strongest version of its own boundary argument: California is plausibly a *favorable* case, which makes its estimates closer to a lower bound than a national average. The state extended its aid deadline by three months; Cal Grant awards are large enough to create unusually strong refiling incentives; CSAC deployed supplementary support when the federal call center failed; and the students most exposed to the SSN failure — undocumented filers — are routed to the CDAA and excluded from the data entirely, leaving only the partially-observed mixed-status population (~10% of applicants) inside the sample. Each of these should make the observed disruption smaller than it would be in a state with a lower state-aid stake, less agency capacity, or an earlier hard deadline. Readers should resist scaling the 7% freshman decline to the nation without adjustment in that direction.

**Standing in the literature and open questions.** On the continuing-student and refiling margin, this is likely the best available evidence on Better FAFSA's first year — it is doing something no aggregate tracker can do, on a question no one else was asking. On the entry margin it is a well-documented state case study that corroborates the national picture with better granularity. It should be read as establishing facts and framing questions rather than as settling effects. What it leaves open is substantial: federal aid receipt and Pell disbursement, which is the channel through which any of this would actually harm students; the fate of the missing freshmen; outcomes for new students, which the authors explicitly acknowledge they cannot observe; and persistence, debt, and completion for affected cohorts. Footnote 8, reporting a strong 2025–26 rebound in California applications, is the most consequential item in the paper for interpretation — it suggests a one-year transitional shock rather than a durable break, and readers citing this paper as evidence of lasting harm from FAFSA simplification should note that the authors themselves say the problems "appear more transitory than permanent."

**Policy recommendations.** Auto-renewal of the FAFSA for returning students follows well from the evidence: refiling is a pure administrative-burden margin, declines were broad and uniform across sectors and student types, and the mechanism is exactly the one auto-renewal removes. The suggestion of college-level mandatory FAFSA submission is weaker. Its supporting citations concern high school mandates, and it sits in direct tension with the paper's own interpretation — if the students who stopped refiling were largely those not returning, a mandate would recover little aid. No estimate of forgone dollars is offered to weigh it. This recommendation reads as editorial rather than derived.

**Overall.** A well-executed, appropriately hedged descriptive study on a timely and consequential policy question, with genuinely new data on a margin the field had overlooked and one finding that deserves further work. It falls short of "strong" not because of poor execution but because the evidence cannot reach the conclusions the paper's most memorable sentences state, and because the two outcomes that would settle its central question — federal aid receipt and new-student enrollment — are absent from the data. Read it as the best current description of what happened in one large state, and as a source of hypotheses rather than effects.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper names its data source clearly and lists its sample restrictions, and the headline descriptive claims can be arithmetically checked against Table 1's Ns — but for a 2026 journal article it carries no data availability statement, no documented access pathway or DUA for the CSAC restricted data, no replication package, and no named software. The central refiling regressions in Tables 2–4 cannot be re-run from the text: the estimator is never stated, the control set is given only as an open-ended "e.g." list, the cohort-definition rule is ambiguous under left-censoring, and no sample sizes are reported for any regression. Two text–table numerical inconsistencies mean even internal verification fails in places, so readers should treat the point estimates as checkable only against the tables, not against the prose.

**Strengths:**

- The data source is named precisely and unambiguously (California Student Aid Commission administrative FAFSA records, four cycles 2021–22 through 2024–25), and the Acknowledgments credit CSAC for access, so a reader knows exactly which agency holds the data and whom a replication request would go to.
- Sample restrictions are enumerated as an explicit list rather than left implicit: exclude self-reported bachelor's holders, keep the most recent transaction per applicant-year, winsorize income at the 5th/95th percentiles, drop the <1% with invalid zip codes, link to ACS five-year zip estimates. This is more construction detail than many descriptive administrative-data papers provide.
- The headline descriptive result is independently checkable from the paper's own Table 1. The reported "just under 1%" overall change reproduces exactly from the Ns (537,112 vs. 533,221 = +0.73%), the −7% freshman decline reproduces from the education-level shares (−7.0%), and footnote 5's population counts (+16,000; −73,000; +87,000) are consistent with the Ns scaled by four — confirming the 25% sample is 25% of applications and giving readers a working internal audit of the descriptive half.
- Footnote 8 points to CSAC's public total-applications page, providing at least one genuinely external, public-data check on the direction of application trends outside the restricted extract.
- The estimating equation is written out with its estimand identified (β2), the clustering level is stated (zip code), and the identifying assumption plus its threats are discussed candidly in the Methods and Discussion, so the inferential logic — as distinct from the computational recipe — is transparent.
- Known data limitations are disclosed rather than buried: loss of income in 2024, absence of individual race/ethnicity, the family-size measurement break in 2024, and the exclusion of California Dream Act applicants are all flagged in the text.
- The authors state their percent changes are rounded to whole numbers deliberately, so as not to overstate precision — an honest reporting choice rather than a documentation gap.

**Weaknesses:**

- No data availability statement anywhere in the article. The Acknowledgments/Funding/Conflicts block contains thanks to CSAC but no access pathway, no data-use agreement description, no statement of whether another researcher could obtain a comparable extract, from whom, under what terms, or with what expected timeline. For a 2026 AERA journal article this is the single largest gap.
- No replication package, no posted code, not even a "code available upon request" line. No software or version is named anywhere — not for the regressions, not for the logistic propensity model, not for the random forest in appendix A4. No random seeds are reported for either the 25% sample draw or the random forest.
- No human-subjects/IRB statement despite individual-level student administrative records linked across years.
- Footnote 3's description of the sample is genuinely ambiguous: "We select 25% of individuals from the sample so they are observed in all years." Read literally this describes a balanced panel of individuals present in every year, which is flatly inconsistent with Table 1's varying Ns (494k–537k) and with refiler shares of 56–60%. The intended meaning is almost certainly person-level (rather than application-level) sampling so that a sampled individual is captured in every year they file — but a replicator has to infer this, and the two readings imply completely different analytic datasets.
- The regression tables report no sample sizes at all. Tables 2, 3, and 4 give point estimates, standard errors, and a baseline rate, but no N for any column, no number of zip-code clusters, and no model fit statistics. Readers cannot assess whether the reported standard errors are plausible, how thin the subgroup cells are (UC and CSU sectors especially), or how much of the sample each panel's conditioning restriction removes.
- The control set is never specified. The text says X includes controls "(e.g., age, income, family size)"; the table notes say "(e.g., age, dependency status, family size) and zip-code-level socioeconomic factors" — two different open-ended lists, neither exhaustive, and neither stating whether the zip controls enter as continuous measures, terciles, or fixed effects. The headline specification cannot be re-run from the description alone.
- The estimator is never named. Outcomes are binary and coefficients are reported in percentage points, implying a linear probability model, but the paper says only "multivariate regression model" — and it uses logistic regression elsewhere, so the reader cannot assume.
- The cohort-definition rule is undocumented where it matters most. The refiling analysis "includes only students who first applied for aid under the prior FAFSA system," with cohorts defined by first filing in 2021, 2022, or 2023. But the data begin in 2021–22, and Table 1 shows "Refiler" is missing for 2021 — so 2021 filers cannot be verified as first-time filers, while 2022 and 2023 first-filers presumably can be (no filing in the observed prior year). This left-censoring makes the reference cohort compositionally different by construction from the two it anchors, which bears directly on how β1 and β2 should be read, and the paper never addresses it.
- The ACS linkage vintage is never stated. "American Community Survey five-year estimates" could be 2017–2021, 2018–2022, or 2019–2023, and it is not said whether one fixed vintage is applied to all four cohorts or vintages are year-matched. Table 1's zip characteristics are identical across all four years to two decimals, which suggests a single fixed vintage — but that is the reader's inference, not the paper's statement. Tercile assignments depend on this choice.
- Tercile construction is undocumented on every dimension that matters: whether zip codes are cut unweighted, population-weighted, or applicant-weighted; whether cuts are computed once and held fixed or recomputed each year. The same applies to the propensity terciles from the appendix A3 logistic model — estimated in 2021–22 and then predicted forward, but whether the tercile cutpoints are the 2021 distribution's or are recut annually is unstated, and the two produce different group compositions.
- The paper's prose contradicts its own tables in at least two places. Discussing Table 2, the text says the freshman refile rate "fell by 1.7 percentage points relative to the 2021 cohort, from a baseline of 57.7% to 56.0%" — but 57.7% is the "All" column baseline; the freshman baseline in the table is 53.1%, so the correct freshman figure is 53.1% to 51.4%, a 3.2% (not 2.9%) relative decline. More seriously, discussing Table 3's Cal Grant terciles the text reports declines of 1.1 pp (4%), 2.9 pp (8%), and 2.0 pp (4%) for the low, middle, and high terciles, while the table reports −0.1 pp, −2.0 pp, and −2.7 pp. Neither the magnitudes nor the ordering match, and the table's low-tercile estimate is statistically indistinguishable from zero whereas the text describes a 1.1-point decline.
- Much of the quantitative claim structure lives in an appendix the main text cannot substitute for. The percent-change figures underlying Figures 1 and 2 are tabulated only in Table A2; the propensity model is only in A3; the random-forest alternative in A4; the enrollment disaggregation in A5; the school-fixed-effects robustness check in A6; the Hispanic-share results in A7. Figures 1 and 2 themselves are cumulative-submission curves from which the cited disaggregated percent changes cannot be read off. The supplemental note is a bare "Supplemental material for this article is available online" with no DOI, repository, or file listing.
- Three overlapping year-labeling conventions run through the refiling analysis — first-filing year (2021/2022/2023), "cohort" label (2022/2023/2024), and academic year (2022–23 through 2024–25) — and the paper switches between them mid-paragraph (e.g., Table 2 rows labeled "2023 Cohort"/"2024 Cohort" while the text says "relative to the 2021 cohort"). This is a substantial and avoidable source of replication error.
- Several construction choices are stated but not pinned down: whether winsorizing is done within year or pooled; what defines a "year" for the "most recent transaction" rule, which is especially consequential in 2024 when ED permitted corrections through late June; how "state aid receipt" and "enrolled" are timed relative to the filing cycle; and, for the zip "non-white share," which ACS table supplies the mutually exclusive race/ethnicity partition (the Table 1 shares sum to ~0.99, implying something like B03002, but this is never said).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat the descriptive half of the paper (total submissions, Figures 1–2, the freshman/sophomore/upper-division split) as the verifiable part. The +0.73% overall change, the −7% freshman decline, and footnote 5's population counts all reproduce from Table 1's own Ns and education-level shares — run that check yourself, it holds. This is the portion of the paper you can lean on without author contact.
- Treat the regression estimates in Tables 2–4 as reportable but not independently verifiable as published. Without sample sizes, cluster counts, a named estimator, or a closed control list, you cannot assess precision, cell thinness, or specification sensitivity. Cite the direction and rough magnitude; do not cite these estimates as precisely identified quantities.
- Do not rely on the prose figures for Table 3's Cal Grant terciles. The text's 1.1 pp / 2.9 pp / 2.0 pp (low/middle/high) contradicts the table's 0.1 / 2.0 / 2.7, and the table's low-tercile estimate is not statistically distinguishable from zero. If you need this result, read it from the table and flag the discrepancy; if it is load-bearing for your argument, write to the authors and ask which is correct. The same applies to the freshman sentence citing a 57.7% baseline that belongs to the "All" column.
- Fetch the online supplement before citing anything about Figures 1–2, the propensity model, the random forest, or the school-fixed-effects robustness. Tables A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, and A7 carry claims the main text asserts but does not display. A reader working from the article alone is taking roughly a third of the quantitative claim structure on trust.
- If you intend to replicate, write to the authors before starting and ask for four things specifically: (1) the exact meaning of footnote 3's 25% selection rule — application-level vs. person-level sampling, and the seed; (2) the full control vector in X, since the text and table notes give two different non-exhaustive lists; (3) the estimator (LPM vs. logit/probit) and the number of zip clusters; (4) the exact rule defining "first filed" for the 2021 cohort given that no pre-2021 filing history is observed. Without all four you will be guessing at choices that move the point estimates.
- Ask CSAC directly about the access pathway rather than inferring one from the paper. The article documents none — no DUA description, no application process, no statement that comparable extracts are available to other researchers. Budget for the possibility that this extract was a bespoke arrangement rather than a standing restricted-access program.
- Before treating the cohort comparison as quasi-experimental, satisfy yourself about the left-censoring asymmetry: the 2021 "first filers" cannot be verified as first-time filers because there is no 2020 data, while later cohorts presumably can be. Since β1 (the 2023-cohort coefficient, reported as consistently positive) is the paper's own placebo-style reassurance, and since the paper elsewhere attributes that positive coefficient to post-COVID recovery, the reference cohort doing double duty as both baseline and composition anomaly deserves scrutiny.
- For a partial external check on the descriptive trends, use the CSAC public applications page cited in footnote 8 alongside the U.S. Department of Education's public FAFSA completion-by-high-school files and National Student Clearinghouse enrollment reports. These will not validate the refiling regressions, but they will tell you whether the aggregate California submission pattern in this paper is consistent with independently published counts.
- If you plan to cite the tercile-based results (income terciles, non-white-share terciles, propensity terciles), recognize that the tercile construction is undocumented in three respects — weighting, whether cuts are fixed or recut annually, and the ACS vintage feeding the zip measures. These are exactly the choices that can flip which zip codes land in the "lowest" group. Cite the qualitative pattern (freshman declines concentrated in predominantly non-white zip codes), not the specific tercile magnitudes.
- Note what is effectively unverifiable as reported: the exact control-adjusted magnitudes in every regression table; the propensity-tercile results (model in an appendix, cut rule unstated, no validation statistics); the random-forest robustness check (no hyperparameters, no seed, appendix-only); and the school-fixed-effects robustness claim in footnote 6, which is asserted in one sentence and shown only in Table A6.
- For readers, not replicators: the paper's substantive conclusions — freshman applications fell sharply, especially in predominantly non-white zip codes, while continuing students' submissions rose, refiling fell modestly, and state aid receipt and public enrollment nonetheless rose — are internally consistent across the tables and consistent with the independent NSC enrollment evidence the paper cites. The transparency problems here bear on the precision and reproducibility of specific numbers, not on the direction of the story.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This is a clearly written, honest descriptive paper whose transparency profile is common in state administrative-data work but has fallen behind 2026 journal-era norms. Three things get conflated in reproducibility assessments and deserve separating: whether the data could be shared (they largely could not, and that is not a failing), whether the access pathway is documented (it is not, and that is), and whether the analytic recipe is documented well enough to re-run given data (it is not, and for the central results that is the binding problem).

**Data availability.** The article carries no data availability statement of any kind. The Acknowledgments thank CSAC "for making these data accessible and supporting this research," which is gratitude, not a pathway. Nothing tells a reader whether CSAC operates a standing researcher-access program, whether a data-use agreement governed this extract and what it permits, whether a comparable 25% sample could be requested by someone else, or whom to contact. The Funding and Declaration of Conflicting Interests blocks are present and complete; the data statement that would sit alongside them in most 2026 journals simply is not there. There is also no human-subjects or IRB statement, notable given individual-level student records linked across four years and linked externally to census geography. Restricted state administrative data legitimately cannot be posted — but a documented reason plus an access route is the modern minimum, and neither appears.

**Code.** There is nothing: no repository, no deposited package, no "available upon request," no named software or version. The paper runs at least three distinct computational procedures — the main linear regressions, a logistic propensity model, and a random forest — and none has an associated environment, package, hyperparameter set, or seed. The 25% sample draw itself has no seed, which means even the sampling step is not reproducible from the paper.

**Sample construction.** This is the most interesting case, because the documentation is better than average in places and ambiguous exactly where ambiguity is most expensive. The restriction list is explicit and helpfully ordered. But footnote 3 — "We select 25% of individuals from the sample so they are observed in all years" — reads literally as a balanced-panel restriction, which cannot be right: Table 1 reports Ns of 510,360 / 494,303 / 533,221 / 537,112 and refiler shares of 56–60%, both flatly inconsistent with a sample of individuals present in every year. The intended meaning is almost certainly that sampling is done at the person level rather than the application level, so that a sampled individual is captured in every year in which they file and panel linkage is preserved. That reading is confirmed indirectly by arithmetic: 25% of California's roughly two million annual FAFSA filers gives about 500,000, matching the Ns, and footnote 5's population figures reproduce as exactly four times the sample differences. But a replicator should not have to reverse-engineer the sampling frame from an implied scaling factor, and the two readings produce entirely different datasets.

Several other construction steps require guesswork. The ACS five-year vintage is never named; Table 1's zip characteristics are identical across all four years to two decimal places, which strongly implies a single fixed vintage applied to every cohort, but the paper never says so and a replicator choosing year-matched vintages would get different tercile assignments. The race/ethnicity partition behind the "non-white share" is not sourced to an ACS table, though the Table 1 shares summing to about 0.99 point to a mutually exclusive classification such as B03002. Winsorizing at the 5th/95th percentiles is stated without saying whether it is within-year or pooled. The "most recent transaction within each year" rule is stated but not defined as to what bounds a year — a materially year-varying construct in 2024, when ED permitted corrections through late June and colleges could not submit individual corrections until then. And tercile construction is undocumented on weighting and on whether cutpoints are fixed or recut annually, for both the zip-characteristic terciles and the propensity terciles.

**Specification transparency.** This is where the paper falls furthest short of re-runnable. The estimating equation is written out and the estimand named, which is good. But the estimator is never stated: outcomes are binary and coefficients are in percentage points, implying a linear probability model, yet the paper uses logistic regression for the propensity model and never says which it uses for the main tables. The control vector is given twice, both times with "e.g." — as "(e.g., age, income, family size)" in the text and "(e.g., age, dependency status, family size) and zip-code-level socioeconomic factors" in the table notes — so a replicator does not know the variable list, does not know whether zip measures enter continuously or as terciles or as fixed effects, and cannot reconcile the two lists. Footnote 4 quietly resolves what would otherwise be a fatal problem — income is unobservable in 2024 but the refiling cohorts are defined by first-filing year, all of which are pre-Better-FAFSA, so controls measured at baseline remain available — but the paper never states that controls are baseline-measured, leaving the reader to infer it. The same logic protects the family-size break in 2024, again only implicitly. Finally, the cohort-definition rule is genuinely underdetermined: with data beginning in 2021–22 and Table 1 showing no refiler measure for 2021, a 2021 "first filer" cannot be distinguished from a continuing filer, while 2022 and 2023 first-filers presumably can be identified by absence in the prior observed year. This asymmetry makes the reference cohort compositionally different from the comparison cohorts by construction, and it bears directly on the positive β1 the paper uses as reassurance.

**Results reporting.** This is where the verification story gets worse rather than better. Tables 2, 3, and 4 report no sample sizes anywhere — not per column, not per panel — and no cluster counts, no fit statistics, no diagnostics. Since Table 4 conditions on prior-year enrollment or prior-year aid receipt within sector, and Table 2 conditions on education level within a cohort-restricted panel, the reader cannot tell how thin the UC and CSU cells are or how much each restriction removes. Standard errors are reported, which is good, but their plausibility cannot be checked against an unreported N.

Most consequentially for readers, the prose contradicts the tables in two places. The Table 2 discussion says the freshman refile rate "fell by 1.7 percentage points... from a baseline of 57.7% to 56.0%" — but 57.7% is the "All" column baseline; the freshman baseline in the table is 53.1%, so the correct statement is 53.1% to 51.4% and the relative decline is 3.2%, not the 2.9% the sentence's own numbers imply. Far more serious, the Table 3 Cal Grant discussion reports declines of 1.1 pp (4%) for the lowest tercile, 2.9 pp (8%) for the middle, and 2.0 pp (4%) for the highest, while the table reports −0.001, −0.020, and −0.027. Neither the magnitudes nor the rank ordering match, and the table's lowest-tercile estimate is statistically indistinguishable from zero while the text asserts a 1.1-point decline. A reader who took the prose at face value would carry away a claim the paper's own table contradicts. Encouragingly, other checkable claims do hold — the Table 3 headline declines of 2.4 and 2.7 pp, the year-over-year swings of 3.3 to 4.3 pp, the dependent-student 65.7% to 63.3% path, and the independent-student 48.9 / 52.3 / 47.8 sequence all reproduce cleanly from the tables — which makes the two failures look like editing errors rather than systematic misreporting. But a reader cannot know which sentences were checked and which were not without doing the arithmetic themselves.

**Appendix dependence.** A structural issue compounds all of this: a large share of the quantitative claim structure has been offloaded to an online appendix that the main text cannot substitute for. The percent changes underlying Figures 1 and 2 are tabulated only in Table A2, and the figures themselves are cumulative-submission curves from which the disaggregated percent changes cannot be read. The propensity model is in A3, the random forest in A4, the dependency-status enrollment disaggregation in A5, the school-fixed-effects robustness in A6, and the Hispanic-share results in A7. The supplemental note is a bare one-line statement with no DOI, repository, or file listing. Readers who do not fetch the supplement are taking a substantial fraction of the paper on trust.

**What the paper does well on verifiability.** The descriptive headline is genuinely auditable from Table 1 alone, and it holds: the overall +0.73%, the −7.0% freshman change, and footnote 5's population counts all reproduce. Footnote 8's link to CSAC's public applications page gives readers a real external anchor. Limitations are disclosed candidly, and the authors explicitly round percent changes to avoid overstating precision. The inferential logic is transparent even where the computational recipe is not.

**Overall.** The assessment is "weak" rather than "insufficient." The descriptive half of the paper is verifiable from what is printed, the data source is unambiguously identified, and the substantive story is internally coherent and consistent with independent enrollment evidence. But the central contribution — the refiling regressions — cannot be re-run from the article by anyone, even with the data in hand, because the estimator, the control set, and the cohort-construction rule are all underspecified and no sample sizes are reported; there is no access pathway documented for the data; there is no code; and at one point the text and table disagree about the sign and significance of a reported result. Confidence is capped because appendix Tables A1–A7 were unavailable to this review and may resolve some of the specification questions flagged here — though a data availability statement, a replication package, and regression Ns are main-article obligations that no appendix would cure.
